articles.title: Russian Commander Complains NATO Testing Drones on Ukraine’s Front Line
articles.body:
In an interview with Russia’s state news agency TASS on Tuesday, Oct. 27 the commander of Moscow’s Akhmat special forces unit, Lt. Gen. Apti Alaudinov complained that NATO nations were using the war in Ukraine to test drone technology in combat against Russia.
He commented that large numbers of Western manufactured unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV) were being encountered: “We see that drones manufactured in all these countries, which are members of the NATO alliance, are being tested against us on the line of engagement.”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Alaudinov claimed that these included drones of every type, capability and operational ranges. According to him, this not only included first-person view (FPV) drones used to attack Russian forces and equipment on the front line but also included long-range UAVs that were being used to carry out deep strikes against towns, cities and infrastructure inside Russia.
The West learning from Ukraine’s experience of drone warfare – a two-way street
In March 2022, in the earliest days of the war, the US Council on Foreign relations commented on how Ukraine relied on drones sourced from Turkey, the Bayraktar TB2, as a means of disrupting Russian tank columns on their march towards Kyiv. Their appearance on the battlefield seemed at first to be a game changer, but it was not long before their vulnerability was exploited by Moscow’s air defenses.
However, the value of drones in taking the war to the enemy and the need for countermeasures was soon appreciated by both sides which led to the battlefield dominance UAVs currently enjoy.
What Israel’s Election Could Change for Ukraine and Relations With Russia
Recent statements by Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense and reports in the Western mainstream and social media seem to partially confirm Alaudinov’s assertions. Ukraine is cooperating with both government and commercial drone-related programs, not only using “attack” and surveillance drones but also to develop counter-drone technology and tactics.
A July report by the Ministry of Defense explained how it was working with NATO’s Allied Command Transformation (ACT) agency using its battlefield experience to support NATO in developing ways to combat drones. The report says this shows that “Ukraine is not only receiving support from its partners but is also actively shaping their approaches to modern warfare.”
On Monday the US publication The Hill reported on comments made by US Air Force Gen. Alexus G. Grynkewich, SACEUR, at a meeting in Poland. This followed on from an earlier report by Bloomberg on plans to use artificial intelligence (AI) enhanced drones to defend the alliance. The general laid out a possible strategy in the event of an attack by Russia, the concept of “blunt, block and break.” The articles suggested that the mass use of UAVs would be key to the success of Grynkewich’s plan and suggested that virtually every military was developing UAV-based concepts supplemented with AI for warfighting.
A week ago, the Wall Street Journal reported on how Ukraine’s “Kill Zone” was being used to test and develop the use of AI in drones. This followed a report in the defense issues website the Defense Post that discussed how Ukraine had been deploying AI tools developed in the NATO-Ukraine Joint Analysis, Training and Education Centre (JATEC) to both plan and control its UAV operations and to predict Russian drone activity. It said a prototype system was undergoing real-time validation by Ukrainian forces.
CBS reported in September that Washington and Kyiv were in the process of agreeing on a policy that would allow the two countries to expand the testing and production of Ukrainian defense technology in the US. It was given new impetus by the use of Iranian drones against US forces in the Middle East.
The report cites experts saying the experience gained by Ukraine in developing drone software and operations, as well as the speed with which it could adapt to battlefield changes, were likely to prove invaluable to the use of drones by the US and its allies.
Deborah Fairlamb, partner in a US venture capital firm that is investing in Ukrainian defense technology, told CBS: “The West needs to start understanding better is that it’s not just about having the tech. It’s about how the tech is used. And this is where Ukraine’s knowledge, skills, experience really need to be transmitted.”
In a separate report on its YouTube channel in July, CBS reported on how Ukraine was deploying US drone technology, such as the “Shield AI” V-Bat vertical take-off and landing (VTOL) reconnaissance and targeting UAV, to support long-range strikes into Russia.

articles.title: Poland to Host €227M Patriot Missile Service Center
articles.body:
Poland has announced that it will be hosting a European service center for US-made PAC-3 interceptor missiles, aiming to cut repair times for weapons that are already in short supply worldwide and critical to Ukraine’s defense against Russian ballistic missile attacks.
Polish Deputy Defense Minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, who led Warsaw’s negotiations, called the decision “historic” in a statement on Tuesday, Oct. 27. Three other countries had competed to host the facility, she said, naming Germany, the Netherlands and Norway.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“This success was not a given. It is the result of many months of negotiations and the hard work of the entire team,” Sobkowiak-Czarnecka wrote, noting that the Polish bid had been the highest rated since the application stage.
According to TVP World citing Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, the hub would be the only one of its kind outside the United States. Its cost would be roughly 1 billion Polish zlotys (about $253 million) and would take about a year to become fully operational.
In her statement, the defense minister thanked Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, who appointed her chief negotiator.
The outcome showed what was possible when the government and the country’s President Karol Nawrocki pulled in the same direction, she added.
Kyiv Plans $22 Million in New Water Crossings Over Dnipro River
Short repair times for scarce interceptors
PAC-3 missiles, used in US-made Patriot air-defense systems, are currently shipped to the US for servicing, which led Washington to seek a European site to cut turnaround times, TVP World reported.
The US, Poland, Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden signed an agreement with manufacturer Lockheed Martin in July, in an aim to explore setting up such a hub.
According to the broadcaster, Warsaw has long pursued the project with hopes that it would eventually lead to Patriot missile production in Poland.
Plant near Warsaw seen as likely site
Although the government did not officially name a location at the time of the report, TVP World reported that the WZE electronics plant in Zielonka, located about 15 kilometers (9.3 miles) northeast of Warsaw, is widely seen as the leading candidate.
In September, Sobkowiak-Czarnecka toured the plant with US Under Secretary of State Thomas DiNanno. At the time, the US Embassy in Warsaw noted that the visit highlighted bilateral cooperation on critical Patriot components.
Under a 2019 agreement with Lockheed Martin, the plant already produces and services key PAC-3 MSE components, TVP World reported.
Ukraine facing critical shortage
As of Oct. 15, Ukraine has reportedly depleted its stocks of Patriot interceptor missiles.
For the country, the PAC-3 is currently among the very few weapons capable of intercepting Russia’s Iskander-M, a ballistic missile carrying a half-ton warhead strong enough to tear down a quarter to half of a typical apartment block.
The shortfall was particularly felt during Russia’s large-scale attack overnight into Wednesday, Oct. 14, when most incoming ballistic missiles reached their targets. The strike hit three power plants in Kyiv and energy facilities in Kharkiv, killing four people and injuring at least 25 in the capital.
According to CNN’s exclusive, Ukraine fired its last remaining Patriots as the Air Force shot down four Russian ballistic missiles during that same attack.
Around the same time, the US aerospace giant Starlink tweaked parameters and limited terminals above 160 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour), crippling Kyiv’s drone operations, including interceptor drones used against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones.
As of Oct. 1, Lockheed Martin is in advanced talks over PAC-3 production outside the US over tripled demand, as countries seek to rebuild their stocks amid the war in Iran and Russia’s escalating rhetoric towards Europe.
For much of the year, Ukraine has repeatedly appealed to its Western partners for faster deliveries of Patriot interceptors.
On Sept. 8, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said Germany would deliver PAC-2 missiles to Ukraine from it’s own Bundeswehr stocks, while Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said contracts are being signed with partners for about 1,000 Patriot missiles.
During the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York, US President Donald Trump said he made a “final decision” to grant Ukraine the licenses to produce Patriot missiles domestically, after backtracking on the previous July commitment.

articles.title: U.S. Air Force puts its first hypersonic missile into production
articles.body:
- The U.S. Air Force awarded Lockheed Martin a $694 million contract to produce and field the ARRW hypersonic missile.
- The service withheld quantities and delivery dates, three years after it had planned to cancel the weapon without production buys.
The U.S. Air Force has put its first hypersonic weapon into production, awarding Lockheed Martin a $694 million contract on Sept. 29 to build and field the AGM-183A Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon, or ARRW, a missile the service had planned to abandon just three years ago, the Department of the Air Force announced on Oct. 26.
The service withheld how many missiles the contract covers and when deliveries will begin, citing operational security, but said the award formally moves the weapon out of prototyping and flight testing and into production. The contract was placed through the Department of War’s Enterprise-Wide Agile Acquisition Contract.
ARRW is a boost-glide weapon that rides a solid-fuel rocket booster to more than five times the speed of sound, about 6,100 km/h (3,800 mph), before releasing a glide vehicle that maneuvers toward its target, which makes it far harder to track and intercept than a conventional ballistic missile. The U.S. Air Force says it will let aircraft strike time-sensitive, heavily defended and high-value targets from long range, outside the reach of enemy air defenses.
“This is a turning point in our advanced weapons roadmap. By moving ARRW from test to production, we’re providing our combatant commanders with a credible, high-speed strike weapon capable of penetrating the most advanced anti-access and area-denial systems,” said Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink.
The missile is too large for most fighters and will initially be carried by the B-52 Stratofortress bomber, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported, and it has also reportedly been tested on the B-1.
“Fielding ARRW enhances our ability to hold targets at risk anywhere around the world. This hypersonic weapon provides the Joint Force a flexible and rapid response option for highly contested environments,” said Chief of Staff of the Air Force Gen. Ken Wilsbach.
The production decision caps a troubled development history. Lockheed won the design contract in 2018, but the first three flight tests starting in 2021 failed before the missile flew successfully in May 2022, and in March 2023 the service’s then top acquisition official, Andrew Hunter, said the program would end without any production buys as the U.S. Air Force shifted its focus to the smaller Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile. The service reversed course in 2025, when then-Chief of Staff Gen. David Allvin told Congress the U.S. Air Force would buy ARRW.
The program received $362 million in fiscal 2026, and the U.S. Air Force has requested $452 million for production in fiscal 2027, although that request is stalled in Congress while the Pentagon operates under a continuing resolution at 2026 funding levels. Budget plans call for $556 million to $621 million a year for ARRW procurement from 2028 to 2031, with missile quantities marked as controlled unclassified information.

articles.title: Kiev makes new demand for European interceptors
articles.body:
Kiev makes new demand for European interceptors
Ukraine has asked five European nations to release 10% of their interceptor missile stockpiles to ease the shortage of air defense ammunition.
Defense Minister Evgeny Khmara presented the proposal by video on Monday to his counterparts from France, Germany, Italy, and the UK, and Polish Deputy Defense Minister Pawel Zalewski, who met in Paris. He said their Patriot and IRIS-T stocks can be replenished from future deliveries contracted for Ukraine with foreign funding.
Khmara floated a similar proposal for advance deliveries of Patriots last month. Kiev also accused Washington of delaying deliveries of the interceptors. US officials cited the competing military needs of their own forces and denied any change in policy toward Ukraine.
The five countries’ joint statement made no commitment to supply additional interceptors, though they reiterated their support for Ukraine “by all available means – politically, militarily and financially.”
Poland and the Netherlands have said they have no Patriot missiles to spare; Greece has warned that aid must not undermine its own defenses. Germany, a key donor, has pledged additional older PAC-2 interceptors from its military stocks. Other European countries have reportedly held back PAC-3 missiles to preserve their own reserves.
The shortage comes amid an escalating exchange of long-range strikes. Kiev intensified drone attacks on Russian oil refineries and retail warehouses over the summer in what Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky called a “40-day pressure campaign.” Russia has said its increased strikes on Ukrainian targets are retaliation. Ukrainian forces are struggling to intercept Russian ballistic missiles and faster, jet-powered long-range drones.
Kiev is also seeking additional financial support after overspending this year. Zelensky has asked European donors for at least €70 billion ($78 billion) to cover military and budget needs; Western governments are struggling to agree on how to finance additional aid.
The EU, which borrowed €90 billion ($100 billion) last year to prop up the government in Kiev for 2026-2027, is facing tensions among member states, with the Czech Republic, Hungary, and Slovakia saying they won’t take part in a potential new loan proposed by the European Commission.

articles.title: Strategic partnership of Poland and Great Britain. Three-Year Defence Cooperation Plan signed.
articles.body:
Strategic partnership of Poland and Great Britain. Three-Year Defence Cooperation Plan signed.
27.10.2026
- The Polish-British alliance has never been as strong as it is today. The agreement we signed, increasing our capabilities and cooperation, is the best example of that. We have signed an agreement on the plan of cooperation in defence. This three-year plan is the result of the Polish-British treaty, signed a few months ago. I am very grateful for this plan of cooperation. It shows our joint involvement: Polish and British soldiers, joint exercises, developing skills. The most important capabilities we are working on are the new technologies, long-range precise strikes, Artificial Intelligence, drones, anti-drone measures, but exercises training our classic capabilities and cooperation in various conditions will be organized based on this defence plan which we have signed today - said the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz.
On 27 October 2026, a bilateral meeting took place in Warsaw between the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, and the Secretary of State for Defence Wes Streeting. The Deputy Minister of National Defence Paweł Zalewski also took part in the talks between the two delegations. The main part of the visit of the British delegation was the signing of the Three-Year Defence Cooperation Plan of the Republic of Poland and the United Kingdom by both ministers.
- Great Britain is an important partner for us when it comes to defence production. The Miecznik programme, whose phases proceed according to schedule, building integrated air defence – Narew, Pilica, Pilica+ programmes, creating an independent production line for 155 mm ammunition – these are just some of our joint initiatives. One of the largest allocations, or our investments in air defence, is being created in cooperation with Great Britain. The selection of submarines by Poland, and deciding on Sweden also happened in cooperation with Great Britain, who will have a large hand in this process. It was one of the most consequential decisions that we have undertaken.
- added the Deputy Prime Minister, noting the most important areas of cooperation.
- We have begun our meeting with the important topic of support for Ukraine. (…) This tyranny, this oppressive, neo-imperial policy of the Russian Federation is a source of harassment for Ukraine since 2014, since the occupation of Crimea and on to the full-scale invasion later. The response of Poland and Great Britain is unambiguous: we will defend liberty with all our might, we will defend our rights and our land, every centimetre of our territory. I believe I can say that during our vis-à-vis meeting the Secretary has proposed a very important message. Among the different international formats, and our ironclad alliances, we have a similar view of the alliance with the United States. Both Poland and Great Britain is in favour of strengthening this transatlantic alliance, and Great Britain is a great example of this – it is from Great Britain that all that is connected to the transatlantic alliance originated. We are in favour of strengthening and building our own capabilities, of greater independence of Europe, but not a disconnect with the United States.
- said the Minister of National Defence.
The signed document maps avenues of strategic cooperation between the Armed Forces of both countries until the end of the decade. The main topics of discussion were matters of adapting the military to hybrid threats, saturating the eastern flank of NATO with modern deterrence potential, as well as strengthening industrial ties. The ministers have also confirmed their unity and coordination in their efforts to support Ukraine.
- This is an important moment in bilateral relations between our countries. The ties of friendship and solidarity between the United Kingdom and Poland go deep, but this is not merely about our shared history – it’s also about our similar assessment of the threats we face today and our joint determination that in this struggle between liberty and tyranny the United Kingdom and Poland will not be passive bystanders. Thanks to the leadership of Poland, its experience and perspective, when Poland calls, the United Kingdom responds. We hear loud and clear what Poland experiences every day, what some call hybrid threats from Russia – I personally prefer to call it state-sponsored terrorism – I see the daily mobilization of your forces and air defence in the face of drone incursions. We are also seeing, not just in Poland but across NATO, how Putin is testing us and tests the determination of NATO. (…) The meaning of what we are doing here today is that it strengthens our capabilities, our defence industry potential and, critically, our alliance. (…) I am thankful for your friendship, support and solidarity. Poland is one of our greatest and, without a doubt, most reliable friends in Europe, and we cherish and nurture this friendship
- noted the British Secretary for Defence Wes Streeting.

In the Dniprovskyi district, shockwaves blew out windows in the intensive care unit of one hospital and two departments of another facility, though no personnel or patients were injured. A separate strike hit a non-residential site near a local supermarket, killing one civilian.
On October 21, the United States restored critical early-warning intelligence sharing with Ukraine regarding Russian ballistic missile launches after a Russian strike hit a 24-story residential building in Kyiv's Sviatoshynskyi district.
The attack struck near the 20th floor, triggering a fire that killed two people and injured two others. articles.title: Two weeks after a Russian supply base burned in Luhansk’s Khrustalnyi, Ukrainian drones came back for an ammo depot
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones blew up a Russian ammunition depot near Khrustalnyi in occupied Luhansk Oblast overnight on 27 October, Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ reported. Drones also hit the oblast’s capital, Luhansk, for hours, and part of the city lost power. Russia’s occupation authorities have not commented.
Russia keeps pushing toward the last big Ukrainian-held cities in Donetsk Oblast. Its artillery there runs on shells kept in rear depots across occupied territory, and those depots sit within reach of Ukraine’s mid-range drones. Each depot lost behind the front pushes Russia to store and move its shells from farther back. That lengthens the supply runs Ukraine’s drones already hunt on the roads of occupied Ukraine.
Secondary detonations near Khrustalnyi lasted over an hour
The drone attack on occupied Luhansk Oblast went on for several hours, Exilenova+ said. Ukraine’s Defense Forces hit the depot near Khrustalnyi, and secondary detonations continued for more than an hour, the channel added. It posted night footage of a large fire glowing on the horizon.
Russia has occupied Khrustalnyi, formerly called Krasnyi Luch, since 2014. The city lies about 65 km southwest of Luhansk. It serves Russian troops as a rear and logistics hub.
Luhansk lost power as drones hit its former airfield
The attack on the city of Luhansk lasted more than four hours, Petro Andriushchenko, head of the Center for the Study of Occupation, said. Residents reported many explosions and fires in several districts, and the power went out. The main strike hit the city’s former airfield, he added. In October 2023, Ukraine’s ATACMS missiles destroyed Russian helicopters at air bases in occupied Luhansk and Berdiansk.
On Yandex Maps, the Russian online mapping service, the struck area near Luhansk airport is blurred, Andriushchenko noted. Yandex blurs military and critical infrastructure sites this way, he wrote.
Exilenova+ also reported a series of explosions in Luhansk. The oblast had been under a mass drone attack for an hour, with dozens of hits in different towns, Ukrainian Telegram channel DroneBomber wrote late on 26 October.
Neither side’s military has mentioned the attack on Luhansk Oblast. Ukraine’s General Staff left it out of its morning report. Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed it downed 222 drones over Russian regions, occupied Crimea, and the Black Sea, without listing Luhansk Oblast.
Pro-Russian local channels confirmed the attack from their side. A channel covering occupied Luhansk Oblast wrote that eyewitnesses saw a large fire and secondary detonations in Khrustalnyi. LIC, the news agency of Russia’s occupation administration in Luhansk Oblast, reported a series of powerful explosions over Luhansk and a visible glow.
The third drone night over occupied Luhansk Oblast in a week
Drones have now hit occupied Luhansk Oblast on three nights in seven days. On 21 October, they struck the seized telecom building in the city of Luhansk that houses the occupation’s mobile operator. Two nights later, strikes cut communications and power in part of the city.
Ukrainian drones just lit up Russian-occupied Crimea, Donetsk, and Luhansk — here’s how (video)
Khrustalnyi itself burned on 12 October, when strikes hit a former motor depot housing Russian troops. Ukraine also hit an ammunition depot there in June 2022. Back then, the site supplied Russia’s offensive on Sievierodonetsk and Lysychansk.
Blasts in Mariupol, Berdiansk, and Melitopol, and Russian claims from Bryansk
Occupied Mariupol heard two waves of explosions overnight, and the power went out after the attack, Andriushchenko also said. In occupied Berdiansk, several blasts near the Ekvator shopping center preceded a large fire, he added.
On the evening of 26 October, strike drones attacked occupied Melitopol in Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Exilenova+ said. Locals also reported FPV drones hitting targets in the city.
In Russia’s city of Bryansk, Governor Yegor Kovalchuk claimed a night drone attack injured six people and damaged three apartment blocks. He said a man also died when a drone-dropped explosive went off. Yevhen Balytskyi, the Russian-installed head of occupied Zaporizhzhia Oblast, claimed a drone hit a Simferopol–Moscow bus near Prymorsk, killing one passenger.
As the attacks began, Russian monitoring resources tracked up to 350 Ukrainian drones in the air, DroneBomber said. Most flew over Bryansk and Oryol oblasts, with more groups near Crimea, Novorossiysk, and occupied Luhansk Oblast.
Ukraine’s drones also weigh on Russia’s road to occupied Crimea. Truck traffic on the R-280 highway from Rostov Oblast has halved to about 1,000 a day because of drone attacks. Anatolii Tsurkin, who heads a carriers’ association set up in occupied Crimea, said so.
Kyiv set aside $113 million for the first phase of a program of middle-strike drones aimed at Russia’s rear. That makes nights like this one likely to keep coming for depots, airfields, and roads across occupied Ukraine.

articles.title: Russia strikes publishing house warehouse in Kharkiv on Ukrainian Language Day, adding to a campaign against Ukrainian literature and culture
articles.body:
Russian forces struck a warehouse belonging to Ukrainian publishing house KSD in Kharkiv on 27 October, disrupting the publisher’s planned November releases. No employees were injured, but the company is still assessing the damage and losses.
The attack came on the Day of Ukrainian Writing and Language, a national holiday celebrating Ukraine’s language and literary heritage. It adds to a series of Russian strikes on Ukrainian publishing houses, printing facilities, and book warehouses that have destroyed millions of books and disrupted the country’s publishing industry.
KSD announced the strike on social media, saying it had planned to greet readers on the holiday and reveal its November releases but instead had to deal with the attack. The publisher said strikes in the area were continuing, preventing it from determining the full extent of the damage.
The company had planned to begin releasing its new books on 5 November. It has now postponed the announcements while it assesses the situation and determines how to proceed.
“We really want to show you the new releases we had prepared for November,” KSD said. “But for now, as we clarify the details, we cannot yet assess the scale of the destruction and understand how we will work going forward.”
The publisher said it would share updates as more information became available.
Russia’s attacks devastate Ukraine’s book industry
KSD’s warehouse is the latest publishing facility affected by Russia’s campaign against Ukraine’s book industry. In July and August alone, Russian attacks destroyed around 13 million books, nearly a third of the number Ukrainian publishers printed in all of 2025, according to the Ukrainian publishing industry.
On 1 August, a Russian strike on a warehouse used by the Ranok publishing group in Kharkiv destroyed around 8 million books, including hundreds of thousands of school textbooks. A separate attack on a printing facility in July destroyed print runs and book materials belonging to numerous Ukrainian publishers.
In October, Russian strikes also damaged a Kyiv warehouse belonging to publisher Knyholav, destroying tens of thousands of books, including titles and reprints that had replaced stock lost in an earlier attack.
Russia has burned millions of Ukrainian books, striking at the infrastructure of Ukrainian culture
These strikes threaten more than publishers’ finances. Destroyed print runs and damaged warehouses delay new releases, deprive readers of Ukrainian-language books, and force publishers to spend scarce resources replacing titles instead of developing new ones.
KSD has not yet disclosed its losses or announced a revised release schedule for its November books.

articles.title: Houthis claim attack on Saudi oil refinery, blasts shake Riyadh
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Yemen's Houthis claim attack on Saudi oil refinery, blasts shake Riyadh
Yemen's Houthis said they targeted Saudi Arabia's biggest oil refinery with a ballistic missile on Tuesday, as blasts shook the capital of the world's top crude exporter.
Saudi Arabia, the Middle East's largest economy, has suffered weeks of strikes from the Iran-backed Houthis against oil and civilian sites including Riyadh's international airport.
"The Yemeni Armed Forces were able to target the Ras Tanura refinery in the Eastern Province with a ballistic missile," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree posted on X, saying the strike caused "massive fires".
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis earlier said it had shot down three missiles fired by the group towards the Eastern Province.
A resident in the city of Al Khobar, south of the Ras Tanura complex, told AFP he heard explosions around dawn and received a text message alert.
"We got the alert on the mobile and then heard a very loud bang," the resident said.
Maritime security agency Vanguard said a fire was reported in the Ras Tanura area in the early hours of Tuesday after an attack.
"The fire has reportedly been contained, while the extent of damage and any impact on oil-loading operations remain unclear at current," Vanguard said.
The Ras Tanura facility along Saudi Arabia's Gulf coast is home to one of the largest refineries in the Middle East and a cornerstone of the kingdom's energy sector.
The complex has a capacity of 550,000 barrels per day. It has been repeatedly targeted by strikes blamed on Iran, including a drone attack in early March that forced a partial shutdown of the refinery.
Meanwhile a series of explosions echoed across the capital, Riyadh, shaking office windows in the city centre. A text message alert warned residents to seek shelter.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it intercepted two ballistic missiles that were fired at Riyadh.
Egypt 'declared war'
Earlier, a Houthi official said the Egyptian parliament's decision to authorise defensive military support for Saudi Arabia amounted to a declaration of war.
Egypt's parliament authorised the measure on Monday, following a request from Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi.
"It is truly remarkable that while these people go to discuss what they call 'peace in the region', Egypt and its parliament declare support for the so-called defence of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and in doing so, declare war against the Republic of Yemen," said Mohammed Ali al-Houthi, a member of the Houthis' political bureau, in a Telegram post.
It was not clear exactly what support was on offer from Egypt, which has the Arab world's largest military.
Al-Houthi's statement also pointed to Monday's visit to Tehran by the Saudi defence minister, Pakistan's army chief and Turkey's intelligence chief, in a bid to de-escalate tensions in the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Riyadh, Ankara and Islamabad recently signed a NATO-style defence pact in Mecca, pledging to consider an attack on one country as an attack on all three.
Turkey and Pakistan have not announced any strikes on the Houthis during the group's weeks of attacks on Saudi Arabia.
'Not afraid of any alliance'
The Houthis said the group was "not afraid of any alliance that may be formed".
Yemen's largely dormant conflict reignited in July, further destabilising the region months into the Middle East war between the United States and Iran.
The Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began hitting its ships, territory and oil facilities, before seizing swathes of Red Sea coastline in a major offensive in September.
The Houthis have in turn reported frequent Saudi strikes targeting areas under their control.
This month the Houthis ramped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, forcing the cancellation of flagship events and shutting down Riyadh's airport for two weeks.
The Houthis' war with the Saudi-led coalition began in 2015, months after they ousted the internationally recognised government from the capital Sanaa in September 2014.

Italy Delays 13th Military Aid Package for Ukraine as Meloni Waits for US Midterms
Italy’s 13th military aid package for Ukraine is ready but remains frozen as Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government waits for the outcome of the US midterm elections, La Repubblica reported on October 27.
The package has already been delayed several times, first from July to September, then until after the League party congress, and now potentially until after the November 3 US vote.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to La Repubblica, the government had previously assured French President Emmanuel Macron and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy that the package would be approved by the end of October. With four days remaining in the month, however, Italy’s parliamentary intelligence committee, Copasir, had still not been called to review the decree.
Italy has not sent a new military aid package to Ukraine since December 2025.
The new package is expected to include Aster 30 missiles, which Ukraine needs to strengthen air defenses protecting Kyiv and other cities from Russian attacks. Italy and France are the only countries able to supply the missiles, according to the report.
Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto has continued to publicly support military assistance to Ukraine and is pressing for approval of the package.
The interministerial decree requires signatures from Crosetto, Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani, and Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti. La Repubblica reported that Giorgetti has been hesitant amid concern over opposition from Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini, though the final political decision rests with Meloni.
Crosetto has privately told colleagues that a political obstacle still needs to be resolved, according to the newspaper. Government officials interpreted this as a lack of final approval from Meloni’s office.
La Repubblica reported that some government sources now favor waiting for the US midterms to assess the direction of President Donald Trump’s next two years and calibrate Italy’s policy accordingly.
Domestic politics are also weighing on the decision. Salvini’s League has opposed further military support for Ukraine, while former Prime Minister Giuseppe Conte has continued campaigning against weapons deliveries.
Italian officials have informally urged Ukrainian counterparts to remain patient, according to La Repubblica, arguing that an immediate confrontation over the package could create additional political difficulties for Meloni.
Italy and France had committed to supplying the missiles by the end of October. With Copasir still not convened to examine the decree, another postponement remains possible.
Earlier, UNITED24 Media reported that Italy’s 13th military aid package was expected to include four SAMP/T NG air defense batteries, Aster 30 interceptor missiles, and seven long-range radars, with part of the Aster 30 stockpile planned for transfer by October.

articles.title: Ukraine intercepting more Russian Geran-4 jet-powered drones, General Staff says
articles.body:
Ukraine's air defenses have intercepted nearly 60% of Russian Geran-4 jet-powered attack drones over the past three months, with interception rates reaching 80% during some attacks, the General Staff of Ukraine's Armed Forces said.
Fighter jets, including F-16s, Mirage aircraft, and MiG-29s, play a significant role in intercepting Russian jet-powered drones, according to the General Staff.
It did not mention interceptions rates of the more advanced Geran-5 drone.
Ukraine is also working to strengthen its short-range air defenses amid a shortage of surface-to-air missiles.
These defenses include Gepard and Shilka anti-aircraft systems, newer platforms such as Skynex, Skyranger, and Terrahawk Paladin, interceptor drones, and mobile fire groups operating across Ukraine's Defense Forces.
Mobile fire groups are equipped with machine guns and man-portable air defense systems (MANPADS), which Ukrainian troops have successfully used to shoot down Russian jet-powered drones.
The General Staff said Ukraine is also seeking cheaper ways to counter the threat, including testing new interceptor drones. Some of the systems being tested have already shot down dozens of Russian jet-powered Geran drones, according to the military.
Russia has increasingly used jet-powered drones to attack Kyiv and the surrounding region since late summer, adding to the threat posed by conventional Shahed-type drones and missiles.
The newer Geran-5 drones fly higher and faster than other drones, making them significantly harder to intercept. Their growing numbers have also challenged Ukraine's existing interceptor drones, which have proved effective against slower Russian drones.
Ukraine is racing to develop faster interceptors to counter the evolving threat, while Russia is expanding production of jet-powered drones.
Ukraine previously achieved interception rates of around 95% against conventional Shahed-type drones.

articles.title: How the War in Iran Could Escalate
articles.body:
President Donald Trump’s conflict with Iran has become a political liability for his administration. Since the last U.S. strikes on Iran fell on Sept. 8, Trump has publicly ruled out attacking Iran before the November midterm elections—and promised to end the conflict after them.
Then, rumblings grew that U.S. and Israeli military planners had reportedly drawn up new strike options against Iran, including the possible use of the largest non-nuclear weapon in the American arsenal: the GBU-43/B, also dubbed “the Mother of All Bombs”.
The targets purportedly would be Iran’s nuclear facilities and energy infrastructure, though there are doubts about whether the bomb could penetrate Iran’s most deeply buried sites. According to these reports, Trump apparently is seeking a strike he could present as a military victory and then end the war without appearing to back down.
But such an approach risks triggering a far wider war than Washington intends. Tehran remains unlikely to let Washington end the conflict quickly and, fearing a potential attack from the U.S., could itself strike first. Either scenario could lead to a new round of fighting far more destructive than the last.
Before the mother of all bombs
Reports of military plans involving “the mother of all bombs” came against the backdrop of two other worrying developments. First, Iran has been escalating its naval attacks, likely in response to increased flows through the Strait of Hormuz. Notably, two UAE-owned cargo ships, the GFS Pride and the Cape Dao, were struck in the Strait as part of this sharp uptick.
Secondly, diplomatic efforts appear to have hit a wall. In late September, Trump rejected the proposal Tehran had put forward on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly: an end to fighting on all fronts, including Lebanon; the lifting of the U.S. naval blockade and oil sanctions; the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets; and the reopening of Hormuz within seven days. Instead, Washington insists that Iran must take steps regarding its nuclear program as part of the package, something Iranian leaders say they will only do at a later stage.
The timing of any U.S.-Israeli attack remains uncertain. While Trump has said he will not resume attacks before the midterms, Israel held its election on Oct. 27, a week earlier, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had reportedly sought renewed fighting before both elections.
American and Israeli objectives may differ, of course. Trump appears to want something he can portray as a spectacular military victory without having to undergo another prolonged war, while Netanyahu’s rhetoric about “finishing the job” suggests more ambitious goals, potentially including toppling the Islamic Republic. Tehran seems to be preparing for either scenario with its own response: a prolonged, region-wide war designed to impose devastating economic costs.
Denying Trump a short war
The dominant perspective in Tehran is that the next war must be fought in a way that makes it so costly that a future U.S. president would not contemplate another. Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesperson for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), said in late September that Iran “will not stop until we have driven the United States out of the region, punished the aggressor, and established permanent deterrence so that no one will dare attack Iran.”
That logic, should it prevail, rules out a symbolic, tit-for-tat exchange. In Tehran’s view, a limited American strike on Pickaxe Mountain, the fortified nuclear site near Natanz that Trump has repeatedly evoked, followed by a limited Iranian response, would send Washington precisely the wrong message: that it can attack Iran’s nuclear facilities, register domestic political gain, and pay a limited, acceptable cost. Iranian officials have therefore warned that even a symbolic, non-lethal strike would trigger a broad response, denying Trump the quick exit he may have asked of his war planners.
Under this scenario, Iran would target regional energy and economic infrastructure. “In a region where we cannot sell oil, no one will sell oil,” Ghalibaf has warned. The UAE is particularly exposed: Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, has accused it of oil “smuggling” in cahoots with U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM). Rezaei also identified new potential targets: undersea cables, data centers, and AI infrastructure in the region, which he claims are worth “more than $2 trillion.” Ghalibaf subsequently extended the threat to regional governments and investors, threatening that anyone providing “funding, equity, land, or energy” to AI companies that “facilitate military aggression” against Iran “will face coercive action.”
If raising the cost of war is the first instrument in Iran’s calculus, duration is the second. Ali Balali, an adviser to the IRGC’s Aerospace Force commander, suggested Iran would conserve its arsenal in preparation for a prolonged confrontation, rather than expend it early. Two days later, Iranian Army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia argued that the enemy’s weak point is a prolonged war.
Timing is a third dimension in Iranian thinking. Iranian military officials have increasingly mentioned the possibility of striking first, preemptively. Akraminia stated that if Iran were to conclude that an attack by the U.S. and/or Israel is imminent, “we will certainly engage in preemptive warfare.” Mehdi Mohammadi, strategic affairs adviser to Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, went further, arguing that a successful strategy requires not only striking first but also delivering a decisive blow capable of “changing the balance.” There is thus at least the possibility that Iran might move early, and then fight long.
That could occur due to miscalculation resulting from ambiguous American and Israeli signals: leaked strike plans, carrier and amphibious deployments, and aircraft approaching but not entering Iranian airspace. Military experts in Iran see this pattern as an effort to normalize military activity and regain the element of surprise. Tehran could thus mistake military signaling for an imminent attack and strike preemptively, even though it may not want another round of war.
The fourth element concerns the range of those Tehran would hold responsible in the event of an attack. On Oct. 5 Ali Abdollahi, chief of staff of Iran’s armed forces, declared that if the United States acted against Iran “directly or indirectly through Israel,” Iranian forces would retaliate against the United States. The warning carries more weight in the wake of Trump’s decision to openly back Netanyahu ahead of Israel’s election. Indeed, some in Tehran interpreted this as a signal that Washington would allow Israel to strike Iran after the midterms. As a result, Tehran has made clear that even were Israel to carry out the attack on its own, U.S. forces and assets in the region would face retaliation.
Widening the map
This interpretation suggests that the scope of Iran’s response to a U.S. strike likely would be far wider. Its conduct in Hormuz since late September offers a preview of how it could broaden the conflict. When the UAE, backed by CENTCOM, kept oil moving through a southern corridor along the Omani coast, the IRGC shifted its attacks from small shuttle tankers to supertankers and stated that vessels using the “illegal corridor” would be “pursued and interdicted across the region.” Strikes followed off the UAE coast and near Qatar. An escalation in the region could drive Iran to go after vital energy and other infrastructure across the Gulf.
Iran’s regional partners also could widen the conflict, although Tehran does not fully control their actions. In Yemen, the Houthis have already opened a second maritime front in the Red Sea, threatening shipping and increasing pressure on Saudi Arabia. In Iraq, Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada, an Iran-backed militia, has threatened to fight if Iran faced an existential threat. The conflict could also extend to Europe through indirect operations.
There may already have been attempts in this vein: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said a suspected September plot near RAF Fairford, a base used by U.S. bombers, was “almost certainly” directed by the IRGC. Tehran denies involvement, but the incident raises the prospect of covert operations against American military assets beyond the Middle East.
Tehran is also preparing for the possibility of a ground operation inside Iran. According to Iranian Army Ground Forces commander Ali Jahanshahi, more than 50 units are deployed along the borders, from the northwest to the Makran coast, and abandoned airfields have been identified as potential enemy landing sites. Iranian security forces have also conducted preemptive operations against Baluch armed groups in the southeast and launched drone and artillery strikes in Kurdish border areas amid concerns that they could open an internal front during an external attack.
A war meant to be the last
Both the U.S. and Iran run the risk of serious misjudgment. The U.S. may believe it can be master of the scope and duration of a war, only to find that Iran holds the key. This power means Iran need not let the conflict end quickly or painlessly.
For its part, Tehran—which survived the fierce exchanges that began in late February, continued through April, and have since become more regionalized—may be convinced that a wider conflict this time again would establish lasting deterrence. But conditions that made this strategy relatively effective in the past have changed, partly because of Iran’s own actions. The more Tehran expands its targets, the more it risks turning neighbors that sought to stay out of the conflict into supporters of its defeat. Saudi Arabia and the UAE have reportedly agreed to coordinate their military support on behalf of anti-Houthi forces in Yemen, while Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has offered to help defend Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks. For the Gulf monarchies, the stakes are becoming existential: either Iran’s leverage is broken, or their access to world markets will remain dependent on Iranian restraint.
In this way, a war intended to deter future American attacks could instead strengthen a regional consensus that Iran must be dealt a serious blow rather than accommodated or bargained with.
Ultimately, diplomacy remains the only way to prevent the gap between American and Iranian perceptions and risk calculus from triggering another, potentially even more costly round of confrontation. Without it, Washington could launch a limited strike expecting a quick exit, or Tehran could strike first fearing an imminent attack. Either scenario could trigger a prolonged regional war that the U.S. wishes to avoid and a growing alliance against the Islamic Republic for which Iran would pay a price.

articles.title: One killed in Ukrainian strike on passenger bus – governor
articles.body:
One killed in Ukrainian strike on passenger bus – governor
A Ukrainian drone strike on a passenger bus bound for Moscow has killed one person and wounded several others, according to Evgeny Balitsky, the governor of Russia’s Zaporozhye Region, where the attack took place.
The attack was reported on Tuesday morning near the town of Primorsk, on the Sea of Azov between the towns of Melitopol and Berdyansk. The area, which Ukraine claims as its territory, lies within the zone of so-called “middle strikes,” where Ukrainian forces have regularly launched drone attacks on purported Russian military and logistics targets using the Starlink satellite system for guidence.
Balitsky said 31 people were aboard the bus, which was traveling from Simferopol, the capital of the Crimean Republic, to Moscow. He said the wounded were taken to hospital, while other survivors were provided with food and accommodation.
The incident comes amid a dispute between Kiev and Elon Musk over Ukraine’s use of his Starlink satellite communications network for military purposes.
Musk has accused Ukraine of abusing Starlink for deadly “middle strike” operations, saying the system was intended as a civilian communications service rather than an offensive military tool. He contrasted it with Starshield, SpaceX’s military-oriented satellite service developed for US government customers.
Media reports and statements by officials have offered conflicting accounts of whether Kiev has direct access to Starshield or relies primarily on civilian Starlink terminals. Kiev has accused Musk and US President Donald Trump of imposing speed restrictions on Starlink terminals that effectively prevented their use on fast-moving platforms involved in middle strikes. Russian media reported a sharp decline in such attacks this month.
While the Ukrainian military depends heavily on Starlink communications, it has other means of conducting strikes deep inside Russia, where Starlink does not normally operate. Long-range drones and missiles can follow pre-programmed routes and use AI-driven final stage guidance to strike Russian energy infrastructure and other stationary targets.
The Starlink dispute has unfolded amid wider tensions between Washington and Kiev over Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil facilities. The Trump administration has repeatedly asked Kiev to curb strikes on refineries amid concerns about rising fuel prices, while Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky has rejected claims that Ukraine’s campaign is contributing to the increase.
Global energy markets are under pressure from several factors, including the US war on Iran, the Ukraine conflict and depleted strategic reserves amid tight crude supplies.

articles.title: Zelensky: Russia fires over 100 ballistic missiles at Kyiv, region in two weeks
articles.body:
Zelensky: Russia fires over 100 ballistic missiles at Kyiv, region in two weeks
President Volodymyr Zelensky said this in a video address, Ukrinform reports.
“And just now, in October alone – since October 14 – there have already been several Russian ballistic missile attacks. Essentially, in two weeks, more than 100 ballistic missiles have been launched against Kyiv and the Kyiv region. We are doing everything possible to protect our energy sector, to protect our infrastructure and our logistics. The task is extremely difficult,” Zelensky said.
The head of state thanked Ukraine’s partners who provide support on time but noted that delays, including in the delivery of missiles for Patriot systems, are making it difficult for Ukraine to protect itself against Russian ballistic missiles.
“If our partners’ support for Ukraine remained just as strong – particularly when it comes to our Patriots and other air defense capabilities – Ukraine would be in a completely different position – a much better one diplomatically as well,” Zelensky said.
The President stressed that Russia continues to attack Ukrainian logistics and urban infrastructure. In particular, during a recent strike on Kyiv, a university campus, residential buildings, a metro station and metro lines were damaged. Russian forces also struck the Southern Bridge, one of the capital’s key logistical arteries.
According to Zelensky, Russian attacks are continuing not only against Kyiv, but also against Dnipro, Zaporizhzhia, Odesa, Kharkiv, Sumy and Kherson.
“It is important that the world sees this, that our partners see it in the United States, on which almost everything concerning Patriots depends, so that we get answers and the necessary authorizations from the Pentagon for Patriot supplies,” the President said.
He added that Ukraine is working to secure new support packages from its partners to protect the energy system, infrastructure and logistics.
As reported by Ukrinform, on October 27, commenting on another Russian attack involving ballistic missiles, President Volodymyr Zelensky stressed that Russia’s targets are energy facilities, logistics and ordinary urban infrastructure.
The day before, he said that Ukraine had been waiting for almost a month for U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth to sign off on missile supplies for Patriot and NASAMS systems.
Photo: Office of the President of Ukraine

articles.title: Russian attacks across Ukraine kill four, injure 55 over past day, as Kyiv comes under ballistic missile assault
articles.body:
Russian attacks across Ukraine kill four, injure 57 over past day, as Kyiv comes under ballistic missile assault
Russian attacks across Ukraine have killed at least four and wounded at least 55 others over the past day, Ukrainian authorities said on Oct. 27, as Russia launched an overnight missile and drone blitz against the capital, Kyiv.
Russian attacks hit Kyiv's Southern Bridge, disrupting metro services, as well as a university campus, an administrative building, and medical centers.
At least one person was killed, and 15 people were injured in the latest Russian attack on the capital, Ukraine's State Emergency Service (DSNS) said. Those injured in the attack include a paramedic, a medical technician, and a 20-year-old university student.
According to the Ukrainian Air Force, Russia attacked Kyiv with an unspecified number of S-400 and Iskander ballistic missiles, launched from Bryansk Oblast, and with 280 strike drones of various types, 69 of which were jet-powered.
Two ballistic missiles and 255 Russian strike drones, including 56 jet-powered drones, were shot down by Ukrainian air defense or suppressed by electronic warfare.
There were 25 locations reported struck by Russian munitions in the capital, as well as 16 locations that were struck by falling debris from downed missiles and drones.
In Chernihiv Oblast, six people, including a 12-year-old child, were injured in a number of Russian attacks, according to regional authorities.
In Chernivtsi Oblast, two men were lightly njured in a Russian drone strike, according to regional authorities.
In Donetsk Oblast, three people were killed and 22 people were injured in a number of Russian attacks, according to regional authorities.
In Kherson Oblast, four people were injured in a number of Russian attacks, according to local authorities. These included a 62-year-old nurse who was injured when a Russian "Molniya" drone struck a hospital in the city of Kherson.
In Sumy Oblast, three people were injured in Russian drone strikes, according to regional authorities.
In Zaporizhia Oblast, five people were injured as a result of Russian attacks, including a 17-year-old boy, according to regional authorities.

articles.title: European countries with the largest defense budgets name Russia their main security threat and pledge continued support for Ukraine
articles.body:
European countries with the largest defense budgets name Russia their main security threat and pledge continued support for Ukraine
Defense ministers from the United Kingdom, Germany, Italy, Poland, and France met in Paris on October 26 as members of the E5 group — the countries with the largest defense budgets — to discuss support for Ukraine ahead of winter.
After the meeting, the ministers named Russia the main long-term threat to European security and pledged to keep supporting Ukraine despite Washington’s warming relations with Moscow.
“Our countries share the assessment that Russia represents the most acute and long-term threat to Euro-Atlantic security and stability,” the final statement reads. Russia’s war against Ukraine and intensifying hybrid attacks in Europe “do not undermine our unity, solidarity and cohesion. On the contrary, they strengthen our determination to pursue the efforts already undertaken to safeguard the integrity and security of Allied territory,” the ministers said.
The ministers pledged to continue backing Ukraine but announced no new military or financial aid packages, Bloomberg said. During the meeting, they limited themselves to reaffirming earlier commitments.
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius stressed that the allies would work to preserve U.S. support for Ukraine: “We will do everything we can to ensure that the U.S. also supports Ukraine with supplies, as well as with intelligence and satellite data.”
The latest deterioration in relations between Ukraine and the United States is forcing Europe to consider how to help Ukraine without American support, Bloomberg said. Pistorius said the E5 countries are also working with Ukraine on their own air defense system meant to supplement the U.S. Patriot systems.
Relations between Kyiv and Washington have deteriorated sharply amid a fuel crisis. Donald Trump first demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian fuel infrastructure, and when a cease-fire could not be reached, he eased sanctions against Russia, allowing diesel fuel to be sold on the world market.
In response, Volodymyr Zelensky accused Trump of trying to force Ukraine into capitulation, saying the United States is delaying shipments of missiles for Patriot air defense systems and restricting the operation of Starlink and Starshield in Ukraine.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
