articles.title: Shoot-down rate of Russian jet-powered drones steadily increasing, General Staff says
articles.body:
Shoot-down rate of Russian jet-powered drones steadily increasing, General Staff says
According to an analysis of the last three months, Ukraine's average shoot-down rate for Russian Geran-4 UAVs is almost 60%, and the interception rate for jet-powered drones is steadily increasing.
Source: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine
Details: The military noted that during individual attacks, the shoot-down rate for jet-powered UAVs can reach 80%.
Quote: "Tactical aviation – F-16, Mirage and MiG-29 aircraft – currently plays a significant role in destroying jet-powered UAVs. At the same time, strengthening our short-range air defence (SHORAD) amid a shortage of surface-to-air guided missiles is a key issue that is currently receiving considerable attention."
Details: The General Staff explained that SHORAD includes anti-aircraft gun systems such as Gepard and Shilka, the latest Skynex, Skyranger and Terrahawk Paladin systems, interceptor drones, and mobile fire groups from all components of the Ukrainian defence forces.
Quote: "Mobile fire groups are equipped not only with machine guns and associated equipment, but also with man-portable air defence systems (MANPADS). Using MANPADS, our warriors are now shooting down the enemy's jet-powered drones quite successfully."
Details: Meanwhile, work is constantly under way to reduce the cost of countering such air threats. In particular, testing of new interceptors is ongoing. According to the General Staff, some models have already shot down "several dozen Russian jet-powered Gerans".
Background:
- Earlier, Ukrainska Pravda reported that the Russians had begun using a modification of the Geran-5 jet-powered UAV called Geran-5 K5-K.
- Two Ukrainian teams are also preparing domestically developed surface-to-air missiles for combat use against Russian jet-powered drones. In addition, Ukraine is already employing seven interceptors that have successfully shot down Russian jet-powered drones.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: injured in Kyiv's Desnianskyi district rises to 12, Russia fires 16 ballistic missiles overnight
articles.body:
The number of people injured due to a Russian strike on the evening of October 26 on the area around Kyoto Park and Lisova metro station in Kyiv's Desniansky district has risen to 12 people, five of whom are students and staff of the State University of Trade and Economics, reported President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
"The number of injured following the Russian strike on the university campus and surrounding area yesterday evening has risen to 12, five of them being university students and staff," Zelenskyy wrote on his Telegram channel on Tuesday.
According to him, while emergency services were helping people and eliminating the consequences of the first strike, the Russians used ballistics again.
"In total, there were 16 ballistic missiles overnight. Plus more than 280 drones. Unfortunately, there are casualties, there were hits in Kyiv, particularly on the Pivdenny Bridge. A serious escalation in the Russian operation against our logistics. There were also strikes in Kyiv, Vinnytsia, Zaporizhia, Dnipropetrovsk, Kharkiv, Odesa, Chernihiv, Sumy, Donetsk, Kherson, and Chernivtsi regions. Almost everywhere, Russian targets are energy, logistics, and ordinary urban infrastructure," Zelenskyy said.
The President of Ukraine emphasized that "artificial and prolonged delays in the supply of interceptor packages for 'Patriots' and 'NASAMS', which unfortunately have occurred recently, directly help Russia achieve the goals of its terror campaign. Every such delay means a new Russian hit on one facility or another."
As Zelenskyy noted, "unfortunately, strikes occur every day. Russia constantly takes new escalatory steps. Pressure on Russia and real support for Ukraine are needed for the situation to change. Thank you to everyone who truly supports our defense of life and understands the value of support packages arriving on time. We must bring peace closer and save lives."

articles.title: Khmara calls on E5 nations to transfer 10% of their air defense missile stocks to Ukraine in exchange for contracted future deliveries
articles.body:
In an address to defense officials from the E5 group (Germany, the United Kingdom, France, Poland, and Italy), Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara proposed that these partners transfer 10% of their existing stocks of interceptor missiles for Patriot and IRIS-T systems to Kyiv. In exchange, Ukraine would offer future deliveries—already contracted and financed via a European Union loan—to replenish those stocks. Khmara also proposed establishing joint production of drones within the territories of these allied nations, the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense reported on Monday.
"We are proposing not just to increase procurement, but to scale up the joint production of Ukrainian drones within the territories of other countries. This will allow us to boost production capacity and provide Ukraine with the necessary drones, while also strengthening the defense capabilities of our partners," Khmara stated.
According to Khmara, Ukraine requires solutions that will bolster the nation's defenses immediately while also enabling long-term defense planning for 2027. The minister identified the strengthening of air defense as the primary critical priority, noting that an immediate exchange—drawing from allies' existing stockpiles in return for future deliveries under Ukraine’s current contracts—would allow for the rapid protection of Ukrainian cities and serve as a model for other nations. Furthermore, Ukraine has an urgent need for man-portable air-defense systems (MANPADS) to counter Russian jet-powered drones; the country is seeking both the transfer of such systems from partners' existing inventories and funding for new acquisitions.
The head of the defense department identified the development of unmanned systems as the second priority, noting that Ukrainian enterprises have the capacity to double their drone production by 2027, provided that funding is delivered on time.
Khmara emphasized that Ukraine strives for a just and lasting peace—a goal that requires strength, readiness to defend the nation, and the timely provision of necessary weaponry to the armed forces.

articles.title: Local ceasefire in besieged Oleshky begins, Ukrainian, Russian officials say
articles.body:
A localized ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky has been "expanded… within Kherson (Oblast)," U.S. First Lady Melania Trump said in a post on social media on Oct. 27.
The ceasefire, which came into effect in the early hours of the morning, initially covered Oleshky and surrounding areas in Kherson Oblast and is meant to allow the safe evacuation of civilians and the delivery of humanitarian aid over the coming days.
Trump did not specify the extent of the expanded ceasefire but Tetiana Shelest, head of communications for Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, told reporters it now covered the entirety of Kherson Oblast.
According to a statement from Lubinets, the ceasefire was being "fully honored," with Ukraine and Russia adhering to the agreement as of 5:30 p.m. on Oct. 27.
"I hope that everything will continue in accordance with the agreed plan and that we will be able to help the civilians in Oleshky who are eagerly awaiting assistance," he added.
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion. Located just across the Dnipro River from Kherson, it has been effectively blockaded by Russian forces, who prevent humanitarian aid from entering.
Residents face severe shortages of food, water, and electricity. Mined roads and constant drone attacks make safe evacuation virtually impossible, and civilians trying to flee on the only roads in and out of the city are frequently targeted by drones.
Trump added that the timing was accelerated by two days to protect civilians and facilitate the delivery of humanitarian aid.
Earlier, Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Office of the President of Ukraine, confirmed a "bilateral ceasefire" began in the embattled Oleshky, in a statement on Oct. 27.
The ceasefire will last until Nov. 1, David Arakhamia, the parliamentary leader of the president's Servant of the People party, said in a later post on social media. Lubinets added that the ceasefire will remain in effect until 10:59 p.m. Kyiv time on Nov. 1.
The agreements were reached in negotiations with Yana Lantratova, head of the Russian negotiating team.
The Russian Defense Ministry announced that Russian forces had stopped fighting in the area in preparation for the humanitarian mission.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Oct. 27 that the Russian military would provide all details of the humanitarian operation in Oleshky, as reported by the Russian state news agency TASS. He added that there were no reports of ceasefire violations as of 11 a.m. Kyiv time.
The Russian-installed head of occupied Kherson Oblast, Volodymyr Saldo, claimed on Oct. 27 that temporary accommodation for residents evacuated from Oleshky had been prepared in the other occupied part of Kherson Oblast, occupied Crimea, and in other Russian regions, Russian media reported.
He added that Oleshky residents will have a choice – either to stay in Russia or to travel to Ukrainian-controlled territory "to reunite with their families."
According to Saldo, the humanitarian mission is scheduled to begin on October 29, while the mined road to Oleshky is currently being cleared.
The Ombudsman's office representatives told Oleshky residents that the demining mission has already started, but the evacuation of the civilians will start on Oct. 30, the Kyiv Independent learned.
The worsening humanitarian crisis in the city has drawn international attention in recent weeks, including from Pope Leo XIV.
Lubinets said on Sept. 16 that more than 6,000 people may remain in Oleshky and the surrounding area, including about 200 children. His office said it had previously verified 358 people who urgently need assistance to leave safely.
In spring 2026, evacuation volunteers still managed to help Oleshky residents leave for other occupied settlements in Kherson Oblast or Ukraine-controlled areas in exhausting multi-day trips through Russia and Belarus. But in recent months, dangers posed by drone attacks, artillery fire, and mined roads have made evacuation by road almost impossible.
Within minutes of the Oleshky ceasefire beginning, Russian forces launched a wave of ballistic missiles at other parts of Ukraine, including Kyiv.

Ukraine Targets Russia’s War Supplies, Troops, and Equipment Across Three Regions
Ukrainian forces struck Russian ammunition depots, supply depots, and concentrations of troops and equipment across the Luhansk, Donetsk, and Zaporizhzhia regions, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine announced on October 27.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The General Staff reported in a Facebook post that Defense Forces units carried out the strikes on October 26 and during the night of October 27. It listed the following targets:
- Russian ammunition depots near Diakove in the Luhansk region and near Ohorodnie in the Donetsk region;
- a concentration of Russian weapons and military equipment near Krasnohorivka in the Donetsk region;
- materiel and supply depots in the areas of Luhansk, Antratsyt, and Tymonove in the Luhansk region;

"The destruction of ammunition reduces the enemy's firepower at the front," the General Staff stated. It added that the loss of stockpiled supplies "hampers the enemy's ability to supply its units."
The General Staff declared that operations against key Russian military targets would continue until Russia's armed aggression against Ukraine ends completely. The post did not provide figures on the damage inflicted or the casualties caused.
The latest strikes follow a similar wave a week earlier, carried out on October 19 and overnight into October 20 across the same three regions. Ukrainian forces then hit a Russian command post near Fedorivka in the Zaporizhzhia region, a military repair unit near Kalmiuske in the Donetsk region, and logistics depots near Kripenskyi, Rivnopil, and Lahidne.
Earlier in October, strikes targeted another repair unit near Chystiakove, a logistics warehouse near Makiivka, and a storage facility near Horodyshche.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Delivery Giant Built Its Own Air Defense—and Says It’s Already Shooting Down Shaheds
articles.body:

Ukraine’s Delivery Giant Built Its Own Air Defense—and Says It’s Already Shooting Down Shaheds
Ukraine’s largest express-delivery company has built its own private air-defense capability—and says it has already shot down Russian Shahed attack drones.
Nova Poshta co-owner Vyacheslav Klymov said that the company is among the relatively small number of Ukrainian businesses to have implemented such a project, according to Interfax-Ukraine on October 27.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“We are one of the few companies that has implemented this project. I don’t want to disclose the numbers, but we have shot down Shaheds,” Klymov said at the Kyiv International Economic Forum.
He argued that private air-defense projects should continue to expand, saying the war has forced large companies to take on functions that would once have been viewed as exclusively the responsibility of the state.
That shift, he said, extends beyond air defense.
Klymov noted that companies can also create their own firefighting units to respond immediately when Russian strikes hit industrial facilities. Nova Poshta employees already extinguish a significant share of fires caused by attacks before Ukraine’s State Emergency Service arrives, he said.
“Large businesses are now looking for fire trucks in Europe so they can create their own services. It’s our property—what’s the problem? Who can forbid me from putting out a fire on my own territory?” Klymov said.
The comments illustrate how Ukraine’s private sector is adapting to a wartime environment in which logistics hubs, warehouses, production sites, and other civilian infrastructure are repeatedly exposed to Russian missile and drone attacks.
Nova Poshta remains Ukraine’s leading express-delivery company, handling documents, parcels, and large palletized cargo across the country.
The company has continued expanding despite the war. In the first half of 2026, its consolidated net profit rose 24.3% year over year to $48 million, while revenue increased 31.8% to $856 million.
As of July 13, 2026, Nova Poshta operated 54,700 service points across Ukraine, including 16,800 branches and 37,900 parcel lockers.
Russia systematically attacks Nova Poshta with the latest strikes affecting branches in Vinnytsia region, wounding eight people, three of whom were taken to intensive care.
Another Russian strike targeted a Nova Poshta logistics terminal in Zaporizhzhia and Dnipro, triggering a large fire at the facility.
Previously, Ukrainian forces revealed a mobile version of the Sky Sentinel robotic anti-aircraft turret, mounting the AI-assisted system on a military vehicle to create a rapidly deployable defense against Shahed-type drones and other low-flying aerial threats.

articles.title: “Our future cannot be the subject of agreements between Trump and Putin”: Ukraine supporters protest US policy on Russia in Europe, US, and Australia
articles.body:
Pro-Ukraine demonstrations took place in more than 10 cities across Europe, North America, and Australia over the past week, with protesters opposing US President Donald Trump’s agreement to resume Russian diesel shipments, the easing of sanctions on Moscow, and restrictions affecting Ukraine’s military support.
The protests were organized by Ukrainian diaspora groups and international supporters of Ukraine, who called on Washington to maintain pressure on the Kremlin, restore Ukraine’s access to Starlink, and stop using military aid and intelligence sharing as leverage against Kyiv.
The International Center for Ukrainian Victory (ICUV) said the actions reflected growing concern over US decisions that could benefit Russia while its war against Ukraine continues.
The demonstrations followed Trump’s announcement on 9 October that Russia would supply diesel to US and global markets. The US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control subsequently issued a temporary license authorizing transactions involving Russian-origin diesel, including imports into the United States, through 7 April 2027.
The decision reversed part of Washington’s restrictions on Russian fuel imposed after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
“We are witnessing a dangerous situation today: Russia, which attacks Ukrainian cities every day, is being offered economic agreements and sanctions relief, while Ukraine is being asked to make concessions. But Ukrainians cannot simply stop fighting. For us, this is a matter of our state’s existence. Our future cannot be the subject of agreements between Trump and Putin. It belongs to Ukrainians,” said Olena Ivashchenko, founder of Campaign for Ukraine.
Protests target Russian fuel deal and pressure on Kyiv
In London, hundreds of protesters gathered outside the US Embassy on 16 October, according to organizers from Campaign for Ukraine and partner groups. Participants included Ukrainians, Britons, Americans, and members of other national communities. British lawmakers also raised the issue in Parliament.
Demonstrators carried signs reading “How Many Ukrainians per Barrel?” and “Occupation Is Not Peace,” calling on Washington to preserve sanctions and reject pressure on Ukraine to make territorial concessions.
Trending Now
Protests also took place in Edinburgh, Chicago, Houston, Boston, San Diego, Prague, Rome, Stockholm, and Sydney. In Prague, two Ukrainian activists staged a protest outside the US Embassy on 21 October, pouring a red liquid resembling blood onto the road to symbolize the human cost of the policy.
Participants in several cities also condemned restrictions on Starlink, delays in ammunition supplies, and disruptions to intelligence sharing with Ukraine.
The diesel agreement has drawn criticism in Ukraine because Russian fuel exports generate revenue for Moscow while its forces continue attacking Ukrainian cities and infrastructure. A Russian diesel tanker carrying 40,000 metric tons of fuel departed Russia’s Baltic port of Primorsk on 22 October bound for New York, according to shipping data reported by Reuters. It was expected to arrive on 7 November.
Organizers warn against easing pressure on Moscow
Protest organizers argued that restoring Russian fuel sales and relaxing sanctions risk helping Moscow finance its war. They also opposed any US effort to secure concessions from Kyiv without requiring Russia to end its aggression.
The demonstrations reflect concerns among Ukraine’s international supporters that Washington’s pursuit of economic agreements with Moscow could undermine efforts to isolate Russia and strengthen Kyiv’s position.
Trump has defended the diesel arrangement as a way to increase fuel supplies and lower prices. His administration has also presented engagement with Moscow as part of its broader effort to end the war, while critics question whether easing economic pressure will produce meaningful concessions from the Kremlin.

articles.title: Britain told to plan for war without Trump’s America
articles.body:
Defence spending should go to five per cent of gross domestic product immediately, the country should be prepared for a wider European war and planning should assume Britain may have to fight without the United States, according to a security academic at the University of Leicester.
Dr Simon Bennett, director of the Civil Safety and Security Unit in the university’s School of Business and author of a 2025 book on security lessons from the war in Ukraine, set out the argument in comments issued through the university press office.
Bennett said: “Given these facts, we must prepare ourselves to fight alone. Like Keir Starmer, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is in denial about Trump. The American president is a lost cause. Better to focus finite energies and budgets first, on supporting Ukraine, and secondly, on preparing this country for a wider European war. Defence spending must be increased to 5% of Gross Domestic Product immediately and, as suggested by former Secretary of State for Defence Lord Hutton of Furness in the 17 October edition of The i Paper, the British public must be told the truth about Russia’s hybrid warfare campaign.”
On the range of threats he believes the country is exposed to, Bennett said: “The United Kingdom faces a spectrum of threats. The country has suffered two Kremlin-initiated chemical warfare attacks, in London in 2006 (Polonium) and in Salisbury in 2018 (Novichok). The Council on Strategic Risks recently highlighted the UK’s vulnerability to biological weapons. Prime Minister Burnham, it is time to focus on what really matters – giving Ukraine the weapons it needs and securing a vulnerable United Kingdom. Do not prostrate yourself before Trump, as your predecessor did. As Volodymyr Zelensky and Mark Carney have shown, the only way to deal with Trump is to stand up to him.”
Bennett is asking for far more than the government has signed up to. Ministers have committed to NATO’s target of three and a half per cent of gross domestic product on core defence by 2035, with a further one and a half per cent on defence-related resilience and infrastructure making up the alliance’s headline five per cent figure. Bennett is calling for core defence spending itself to reach five per cent now, a distinction ministers have had to set out repeatedly.
Lord Hutton of Furness, whose intervention Bennett cites, was Secretary of State for Defence from 2008 to 2009. His argument that the public must be told the truth about Russian hybrid warfare runs close to what ministers have themselves begun saying. Wes Streeting told the Defence Committee this month that hybrid activity of this kind amounts to state backed terrorism, and Louise Sandher-Jones confirmed in a written answer last week that “we know Russia is conducting a campaign of hybrid attacks and sabotage across Europe.”
Ministers have also confirmed that government messaging on defence and security will build ahead of Exercise ALBISTON SHADOW and NATO’s crisis management exercise in spring 2027, and the Cabinet Office launched its Be Ready campaign this month asking households to prepare to look after themselves for three days.
The two chemical incidents Bennett refers to are the poisoning of Alexander Litvinenko with polonium-210 in London in 2006, which a public inquiry found was probably approved by the Russian president, and the Novichok attack on Sergei and Yulia Skripal in Salisbury in 2018, which killed Dawn Sturgess and which Britain attributed to the GRU. The Council on Strategic Risks is a Washington-based institute publishing on biological, climate and nuclear security.
Bennett’s case rests on his reading of the American president, whom he describes as a Russophile and, in his words and expressly as his opinion, a traitor to the West’s liberal-democratic values. He said he predicted in March 2025 that Trump would ally the United States with Russia through accords and treaties, and took criticism for saying so at the time.

articles.title: A 4-watt video link passed Ukraine’s state tests, its maker says, and could stretch STING interceptors’ radius from 20 km to 30 km
articles.body:
A new video transmitter for Wild Hornets’ drones, including its STING interceptors, has passed state tests, the Ukrainian drone maker told Militarnyi. The module sends a drone’s camera feed to its pilot. The company expects it to widen its interceptors’ operating radius.
Russia launched 140 Shahed-type drones at Ukraine overnight on 26 October and 280 the next night, when its main target was Kyiv, Air Force figures as of the morning show. Interceptor drones, which cost dozens of times less than the Shaheds they hunt, are one of Ukraine’s answers. The STING alone downed more than 3,000 drones in its first seven months of use, Wild Hornets says. If the company’s estimate holds, a 30 km radius would let each ground station cover more than twice the area it covers at 20 km.
What the testers checked
Specialists from the State Research Institute for Testing and Certification of Arms and Military Equipment and the Defense Ministry’s State Quality Assurance Directorate confirmed the module’s declared characteristics on three drone types, the company said. The three were the STING interceptor, the Queen of Hornets cargo platform, and the 10-inch Wild Hornets Digital anti-aircraft drone.
Some of the drones’ figures exceeded the values the company had set for them, Wild Hornets told Ukrainian defense outlet Oboronka, without saying which ones. Those figures will enter the official specifications after further field tests, it said.
More than double the power
The module, called HV VTX Pro, is part of an upgrade to Wild Hornets’ Hornet Vision digital video system. It more than doubles the transmitter’s maximum power, to 4 W. That sends a clear picture farther and makes the feed steadier in crowded airwaves and under electronic jamming, the company said.
Wild Hornets first described the module in August, when it was already in serial production. Its interceptors’ operating radius would grow from around 20 km to 30 km, the company said at the time. That estimate assumed good line of sight and the 360-degree antenna on its ground stations, according to a company statement Interfax-Ukraine quoted. Interception could also become at least 20% more effective against targets flying extremely low, the statement said.
Wild Hornets is a Ukrainian company that designs and builds drones, from strike FPV drones and cargo platforms to the STING, which the company says flies at up to 280 km/h to hunt Shaheds. Its drones serve with more than 100 units of Ukraine’s Defense Forces, from the army and the National Guard to military intelligence, the Air Force, and the border guard, according to Interfax-Ukraine.

articles.title: Nordic call to Putin opens rift in Europe on Ukraine
articles.body:
Nordic call to Putin opens rift in Europe on Ukraine
A phone call with the leaders of Finland and Norway’s with Russian President Vladimir Putin has exposed divisions among Ukraine’s European backers. Denmark criticized the initiative and Sweden complained that it had received no advance notice.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store contacted Putin on Tuesday ahead of renewed Russia-US-Ukraine peace talks in Abu Dhabi next month. The leaders discussed efforts to resolve the conflict, as well as security and stability in Northern Europe and the Baltic Sea.
Most Western European leaders have shunned direct contact with Moscow since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022, but now appear to be desperately seeking a seat at the negotiations table. Both Stubb and Store have been named as potential candidates to represent Brussels at the talks, but neither spoke on Europe’s behalf during Tuesday’s call.
Following the conversation, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen accused her Nordic colleagues of breaking ranks, saying she was “very skeptical about this Norwegian-Finnish initiative” because it had “not been coordinated with the rest of us.”
Frederiksen said Europe should stick together rather than go solo, doubting anything can be achieved through unilateral contacts with Moscow.
Her opposition to the diplomatic initiative comes as Copenhagen is backing Kiev’s efforts to expand its weapons production to Danish soil. Ukrainian arms manufacturer Fire Point plans to build a missile-fuel factory in Denmark.
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson also lamented that he had not been informed of the call to Putin beforehand and said he had “pretty low expectations for this kind of conversation.”
Western leaders have repeatedly faced backlash for contacting Putin or advocating direct talks with Moscow. Earlier this year, Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever sparked a wave of backlash from his colleagues after arguing that Europe’s strategy of arming Kiev and sanctioning Russia had failed, leaving negotiations as the only viable option.
His comments elicited an immediate retort by EU Foreign Policy chief Kaja Kallas, who has consistently dragged the bloc down the warpath with Russia. She argued that normalizing ties with Moscow would lead to “more wars.” De Wever’s own foreign minister also described the move as “a signal of weakness.”
In 2024, then-German Chancellor Olaf Scholz was also accused of opening a “Pandora’s box” by calling Putin, with Estonia and other Baltic states decrying contacts with Moscow a “strategic mistake.”
Russian officials have repeatedly accused European governments of prolonging the conflict and obstructing a settlement while demanding a place at the negotiating table. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said in March that the EU had “completely discredited itself” as a mediator, citing its failure to uphold previous agreements and its support for deploying Western troops in Ukraine.
Moscow has nevertheless expressed willingness to engage with a European representative committed to negotiations. On Sunday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said a negotiator from Brussels would be welcome, but stressed that such a person would need to be “someone genuinely committed to facilitating a peaceful settlement.”

articles.title: Iraq: Drone shot down near US embassy in Baghdad
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iraq: Drone shot down near US embassy in Baghdad
A drone was shot down near the US embassy in Baghdad on Tuesday, triggering three loud explosions near the heavily fortified Green Zone, Iraqi security officials said.
Iraq's Security Media Cell said in a brief statement that the explosions were caused by the interception of a drone near the Green Zone, which houses the US embassy and several government institutions.
Security sources in Baghdad told The New Arab that two surveillance drones had approached the US embassy compound before being intercepted by its C-RAM air defence system.
The sources said Iraqi authorities had launched an investigation but had not yet established where the drones were launched from.
The incident comes as the Iraqi government continues efforts to persuade armed factions to surrender their weapons and bring all military capabilities under state control.
Several factions have agreed to hand over their weapons, but others have refused, including four groups operating under the umbrella of the Islamic Resistance in Iraq.
They are Kataib Hezbollah, Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada, Harakat al-Nujaba and Harakat al-Awfiya.
Security sources told The New Arab that they suspected the drones belonged to factions opposed to disarmament, although no group had claimed responsibility.
The sources said the factions continued to regard the US embassy as an occupation base and possessed surveillance and drone capabilities unmatched by other local Iraqi groups.
Last week, the four factions accused Washington of violating Iraqi sovereignty and failing to honour its commitments to Baghdad.
In a joint statement, they criticised restrictions on airports and border crossings with Iran, arguing that such decisions were being dictated by the United States.
They also questioned whether Iraq could exercise genuine sovereignty while major national decisions remained subject to foreign influence.
Earlier, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi announced that three of five armed factions that had agreed to surrender their weapons had already done so, while negotiations continued with the remaining two.
"Five factions agreed to hand over their weapons, and three have already done so, while dialogue continues with the others," Zaidi said during a meeting with tribal leaders, according to his office.
Iraqi researcher Mujashaa al-Tamimi told The New Arab that the use of surveillance drones could be intended to signal to Washington that armed factions remained active and capable of carrying out operations.
However, he stressed that this interpretation depended on whether the drones had actually been launched by those groups.
Tamimi warned that the renewed use of drones could signal another period of heightened tensions in Baghdad.

articles.title: Iran opposes nuclear technology monopoly, calls for equal access to advanced technologies
articles.body:
Iran opposes nuclear technology monopoly, calls for equal access to advanced technologies
TEHRAN — Iran has called for equitable global access to advanced nuclear technologies, urging the international community to eliminate discriminatory barriers, expand technical cooperation and strengthen protections for peaceful nuclear facilities.
Hossein Derakhshandeh, deputy head of the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran (AEOI) and chief executive of the Nuclear Power Production and Development Company of Iran, outlined four priorities for the equitable development of nuclear power at the International Ministerial Conference on Nuclear Power in South Korea on Tuesday.
He stressed the need to remove discriminatory restrictions, facilitate access to advanced technologies, broaden technical cooperation and reinforce international measures to protect peaceful nuclear facilities, warning against the use of nuclear technology to establish monopolies.
Derakhshandeh also called for equal access to advanced nuclear technologies in accordance with international law and without double standards. He reaffirmed the inalienable right of states party to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) to conduct nuclear research and development and use nuclear energy for peaceful purposes.
Emphasizing the importance of upholding the rights of NPT signatories, he called on the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) to function as an independent, technically focused and development-oriented organization, in line with its Statute. The Agency’s mandate includes promoting the peaceful use of nuclear energy and facilitating technical cooperation among member states without discrimination, he said.
However, Derakhshandeh argued that developments in recent years had shown the Agency to be increasingly influenced by political considerations, undermining its impartial implementation of its statutory responsibilities. He cited the US-Israeli attacks on Iran’s peaceful nuclear facilities as an example of the challenges facing the international nuclear framework.
He described the attacks as a flagrant violation of the United Nations Charter, international law, and IAEA General Conference resolutions prohibiting attacks on peaceful nuclear facilities. He also criticized the Agency for an 'inadequate response,' saying it had failed to uphold the fundamental principles of impartiality and professionalism effectively.
Derakhshandeh stressed that protecting peaceful nuclear infrastructure was a shared international responsibility. He also condemned 'international silence over violations of the Iranian people’s rights' in areas including energy, healthcare, food security, the environment and industry.
He further criticized the Israeli regime, the United States and certain European countries for 'politically motivated campaigns' against Iran, involving unfounded accusations and negative media coverage.
His remarks underscored Iran’s call for a nuclear order grounded in equal access to technology, respect for the peaceful-use rights of NPT signatories. and the consistent application of international law, free from political pressure and discriminatory treatment.

articles.title: Iraq PM sacks spy chief as provincial leader faces legal action
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iraq PM sacks intelligence chief as provincial leader released after arrest warrant over civil disobedience threats
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has removed the head of the country’s National Intelligence Service, while a Baghdad court has issued an arrest warrant for the chairman of a southern provincial council over threats to start civil disobedience in protest against the closure of a border crossing with Iran.
The state news agency INA reported on Monday that al-Zaidi had ordered the termination of Hamid al-Shatri’s appointment as head of the National Intelligence Service. Al-Shatri had held the post since December 2024.
The agency did not provide a reason for the decision or name a successor.
Separately, the Third Karkh Investigative Court issued an arrest warrant for Maysan Provincial Council chairman Mustafa al-Muhammadawi, following a complaint submitted by the prime minister’s office over his threat to declare civil disobedience and block roads unless the government reopened Al-Sheeb border crossing with Iran.
Al-Muhammadawi was later released by the court on Tuesday after complying with the relevant legal procedures, his office said, according to the privately-owned National Iraqi News Agency (NINA).
The legal action followed remarks al-Muhammadawi made during a news conference at the crossing on Sunday, when he gave the federal government until 29 October to reopen it. He threatened to declare civil disobedience and block major roads if the government failed to meet his demand and used language that al-Zaidi’s media office described as inappropriate.
Al-Zaidi ordered an investigation into the remarks on Monday. His office said the move was intended to ensure compliance with the law and constitutional and administrative procedures when dealing with public service and administrative matters. It added that the relevant authorities would determine any legal responsibility arising from the statements.
Dozens of protesters also blocked the nearby Bazargan road, a key route used by oil companies in Maysan, in protest against the continued closure of the crossing. Security forces were deployed around the demonstrations.
Members of Maysan Provincial Council have warned that the closure could have serious consequences for the province’s economy and residents’ livelihoods and called on the government to reopen the crossing.
The Iraqi government ordered the closure of Al-Sheeb crossing on 20 October, with the suspension taking effect the following morning and remaining in place until further notice. Baghdad said the move was intended to improve the crossing’s technical and logistical readiness. An Iraqi border official separately told Reuters that security measures at the crossing were weak and inadequate.
The decision prompted criticism from Iran’s Interior Ministry, which said Tehran had not received prior notification from Baghdad.
Iraq also ordered the temporary closure of the Shalamcheh border crossing with Iran in September as a precaution following drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, according to Iraqi security sources. Riyadh said the drones had been launched from Iraqi territory.
On 28 July, joint US-Saudi airstrikes targeted Iran-backed militias in Iraq, which they said were reportedly responsible for attacks on US forces and Saudi energy infrastructure.
Wider government shake-up
Separately, al-Zaidi has ended the contracts of 69 advisers, experts and other staff working in his office, as part of a wider government shake-up that has also included a change at the top of the prime minister’s office.
INA reported on Monday that the decision was set out in an administrative order dated 22 October, which cited the “public interest” but did not provide specific reasons for ending the appointments.
Records reviewed by 964media news site showed that the affected positions covered areas including security, foreign affairs, economic policy, health, education and public administration. Paid posts carried salaries of between one million and five million Iraqi dinars, while several contracts were unpaid.
Some of those dismissed had worked in the office for several years, while others had contracts due to run until 2027.
The list also included political figures, former ministers and judges, The New Arab had learned. The appointments had generated additional costs, including allowances for protection, accommodation and transport.
The prime minister’s office director, Ihsan al-Awadi, was also replaced by Rashad Khalaf Hashim, who took over at a handover ceremony on Monday.
Bloated public sector
The changes come amid expectations of further dismissals and retirements across Iraqi ministries and state institutions.
An unnamed official at the prime minister’s office told The New Arab that the government would begin a campaign to address excessive employment in the public sector, using performance assessments to determine whether officials should remain in their positions or leave public service.
The official said there was broad political agreement on the measures, which would extend beyond Baghdad to include ministries, security institutions and provincial administrations. A recent government review had identified dozens of surplus positions draining the state’s operating budget, some of which had been created under previous governments as political or personal favours rather than to meet administrative needs.
Iraqi political affairs expert Ahmed Ali al-Hamdani told The New Arab that at least 30 other advisers had been retained because they performed actual duties within the government office.
He said some of those whose contracts were terminated had remained in government for as long as 19 years without producing research, policy proposals or ideas, adding that many of the appointments had been made for political reasons.
Al-Hamdani also said the list included the daughter of a former president, the son of a minister, former lawmakers and ministers, and politicians who had lost elections but were subsequently appointed as advisers.

articles.title: What сomes after the war: Bosnia's lesson for Ukraine
articles.body:
What сomes after the war: Bosnia's lesson for Ukraine
This op-ed was co-authored with Kateryna Kyrychenko, a Ukrainian international lawyer and Head of Ukraine Legal Affairs and Programme Management at the Public International Law & Policy Group (PILPG). Her work covers international criminal law, accountability for Russian war crimes, peace negotiations and transitional justice. She is pursuing a PhD in international criminal law at the National University of Kyiv-Mohyla Academy.
On a sunny September afternoon, Kyiv almost seemed at peace. People sat outside the Food Market, talking and eating. Between meetings, we discussed Bosnia's and Ukraine's shared experience. For one of us, war is a memory shaping life three decades later; for the other, an immediate reality of air-raid alerts, sleepless nights and uncertainty about the next Russian attack. We returned to one question: what does it mean for war to end?
A month earlier in Sarajevo, a meeting with Ukrainian officials and civil-society representatives had focused on how Bosnia and Herzegovina handled post-war return and reconstruction. Families crossed former front lines to reclaim homes; property disputes took years, and people returned to areas governed by forces that had driven them out. These challenges are familiar to Bosnians. For Ukrainians still at war, the question was not simply how people had managed to return, but what it had taken to rebuild their lives in places from which they had once been driven.
Pressure to negotiate is mounting in Kyiv, yet little attention goes to a peace framework with credible guarantees. After more than 12 years of Russian aggression, including nearly five of full-scale invasion, Ukraine's weariness is understandable. Millions have lost homes, loved ones or livelihoods; families have been separated for years, and communities live between air-raid alerts and the next attack. They want the war to end, but exhaustion is not willingness to accept peace at any price. Distant negotiators may see this desire for relief as a chance for a quick deal. What seems a breakthrough in Washington or a European capital can have different consequences for those living with its terms. Bosnia shows the gap between signing an agreement and the reality that follows.
Ending the war is only the beginning
Dayton, Ohio, is remembered for producing the 1995 peace agreement that ended the Bosnian war. Its annexes covered the constitution, military arrangements, elections, human rights and refugee return. Unlike an archived document, it had force behind it: some 60,000 NATO-led Implementation Force (IFOR) troops separated armies, oversaw territorial transfers and enforced military provisions. Peace required troops on the ground, and the money and governments willing to keep them involved after Bosnia left the front pages.
Ukraine knows the limits of a mission without enforcement powers. From March 2014, the OSCE Special Monitoring Mission monitored the security situation, established facts and reported violations, while also facilitating dialogue and supporting local ceasefire arrangements; it had no power to enforce compliance. Its mandate expired on 31 March 2022 because OSCE consensus on an extension could not be reached owing to Russia's position. The Minsk agreements, meant to end hostilities in eastern Ukraine, proved vulnerable to manipulation: repeated ceasefire violations, unresolved security questions and incompatible readings of political provisions. They neither secured peace nor prevented Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. For Ukraine, the question is not whether another agreement can be signed but what would make it different from arrangements Russia has already violated: who would verify compliance, respond to renewed attacks and impose consequences?
Dayton was possible under different conditions: the parties accepted IFOR's deployment and undertook to facilitate its operations, while the UN Security Council authorised the force. Russia, by contrast, is Ukraine's aggressor and holds a UN Security Council veto. A guarantee it can veto offers little protection. Ukraine's security cannot rest on monitoring or diplomatic assurances: its ability to defend itself, maintain military capabilities and choose security partnerships must be central to any settlement. Restricting its self-defence while Russia can rearm risks another war.
Civilian implementation was equally demanding. Dayton created the Office of the High Representative, but implementation soon exposed serious obstacles. In December 1997, the Peace Implementation Council in Bonn supported the exercise of what became known as the Bonn Powers: the High Representative could impose binding decisions on specified implementation issues and remove officials who obstructed Dayton commitments.
Ukraine faces a less favourable international environment. Beyond Russia's veto, other major powers' interests may not align with its security needs. Those conditions cannot simply be recreated. Proposals for Ukraine must start from this reality, not assume guarantees will enforce themselves.
The unfinished business of peace
Property return showed that work went beyond the text. Annex 7 gave refugees and displaced people the right to return home and have their property restored, or to receive compensation where restoration was impossible. Laws and administrative procedures were developed and enforced, with municipalities monitored and pressed to comply. People could receive house keys yet find the hardest part of return ahead. For some returnees, especially those returning as an ethnic minority, the label "returnee" can be a reminder that the return of property does not necessarily restore their place in society.
Much will be familiar in Ukraine: destroyed or occupied homes, separated families and repeated displacement. The scale of destruction, mines and unexploded ordnance, displacement of millions and Russia's systematic efforts to alter the demographic, legal and cultural realities of occupied territories will compound Ukraine's challenges. Restoring Ukrainian governance requires more than replacing flags or reopening offices. It must address documented pressure to obtain Russian citizenship, property expropriation, the replacement of Ukrainian education and the suppression of Ukrainian identity, forcible transfers or deportations of civilians, including children, to the Russian Federation, arbitrary detention by Russian forces or occupation authorities, and the consequences of occupation.
War's end brings difficulties beyond rebuilding homes and institutions: disputes over education, integration, national symbols, history, heroes and victims. Who decides what schools teach, whose suffering is recognised and whose history becomes official? Bosnia has grappled with these issues since 1995; many remain unresolved. Survivors and victims' families still face denial of the Srebrenica genocide, historical revisionism and glorification of convicted war criminals, according to the Srebrenica Memorial. Reconciliation efforts have sometimes emphasised moving forward rather than confronting the past. Ukraine should heed the warning: ending a war and reconciling societies are different things.
Despite its achievements, Dayton left unresolved questions, notably the struggle over the Bosnian state. Its two entities and political system enabled obstruction and challenged state authority. Bosnia's experience is not a warning against decentralisation or minority rights. Nevertheless, trouble begins when arrangements protecting communities let a neighbouring government prevent a country from deciding for itself. For Ukraine, a Russian veto over defence or European integration would be especially dangerous. Russia has sought to use the status of occupied territories to influence Ukraine's internal affairs. A settlement must not institutionalise that interference as political compromise or minority protection.
What happens after the diplomats leave?
We sought no Ukrainian version of Dayton. and Dayton's unfinished business in Bosnia makes it no blueprint. But it stopped the war, and some people returned and homes were rebuilt because outsiders stayed to enforce commitments local politicians resisted.
Ukraine's partners should ask what they will do on the first day after the war, not just what they will sign, propose or pressure others to accept. Bosnians understand Ukraine's reluctance to accept promises without guarantees: they have been down that road and, in many ways, still are.
These answers will matter years later, when another crisis dominates headlines and Ukraine leaves the global spotlight. Who will remain engaged, provide assistance or step in when agreements are violated or institutions fail?
"At least nobody's shooting" was common in post-war Bosnia. It is a painfully modest definition of peace, hardly a foundation for the future, especially for those living with unresolved consequences.
Nedim Jahić and Kateryna Kyrychenko

articles.title: The threat looming over Sweden: how the country is preparing for a possible war and learning from Ukraine
articles.body:
The threat looming over Sweden: how the country is preparing for a possible war and learning from Ukraine
Sweden's support for Ukraine is unprecedented. The governing coalition and opposition are united in their political backing, and the public is wholeheartedly rooting for Ukraine to win. Blue and yellow flags are visible throughout Stockholm, solidarity events take place regularly, and Ukrainians can use public transport free of charge. With the February aid package included, Sweden's total military assistance to Ukraine has reached SEK 128 billion (over €11 billion).
However, as tensions escalate in the Baltic region, concern is growing within Sweden itself. At a meeting with journalists in Stockholm, Ukraine's Ambassador to Sweden, Svitlana Zalishchuk, highlighted the persistent cyber threat to Swedish infrastructure.
Sweden regularly records incursions into its airspace by Russian fighter jets and the presence of Russian submarines near key maritime routes. Espionage is also becoming an increasingly pressing concern: suspicious individuals are more frequently seen photographing and filming critical infrastructure. Stockholm recognises that these are not isolated incidents, but part of Russia's broader preparations for hybrid warfare.
This is precisely why Sweden relies on its unique concept of Total Defence, which was officially reintroduced in 2015, following Russia's annexation of Crimea and the start of its aggression in Ukraine's east.
Every state agency and local authority has a clearly defined protocol to follow if the situation escalates. Emergency preparedness drills are compulsory for all organisations, with no exceptions, and are held annually. The country also regularly tests its mass alert system. I happened to hear it last summer while visiting a friend in Uppsala. The siren has an unusual, low, muffled sound, somewhat like the distant rumble of heavy lorries.
In a crisis, national radio will serve as a vital link between the state and the public. Sweden's official preparedness leaflet, In case of crisis or war, which is distributed to every home by the Swedish Civil Defence and Resilience Agency, lists a battery-powered radio among the essential items people should keep at home. It is Sveriges Radio (P4 channel) that has been designated as the official source of emergency information, which will continue broadcasting even in the event of a total blackout or a communications collapse.
Sweden's public broadcaster is now looking closely at how Ukraine has managed to keep broadcasting throughout the war. At meetings with Sveriges Radio's management, including Director-General Cilla Benkö and her deputy, Gabriel Byström, the focus was on practical solutions: ensuring newsrooms can operate without a reliable power supply, keeping broadcasts on air during bombardments and protecting journalists from burnout.
Commercial media outlets are not lagging behind either. Fredrik Malmberg, head of news at TV4, one of Sweden's largest television networks, said the channel has drawn up several contingency plans for wartime operations – right down to setting up backup offices for teams in the event of an attack on its main broadcasting facilities.
Sweden set up its own Psychological Defence Agency in 2022 to counter disinformation and study hostile information campaigns and psychological operations. In collaboration with Fojo Media Institute, the agency provides specialist training for professional journalists. Leading editorial offices, meanwhile, have been designated as high-alert facilities.
Ukraine remains a prominent subject in Swedish media outlets, regardless of their political leanings. Aftonbladet, one of Sweden's leading centre-left newspapers, published an op-ed with the telling headline "A Russian victory will cost twice as much as aid to Ukraine", openly urging the government to commit at least 1% of GDP to supporting Ukraine and to invest in its victory, not merely its survival.
Meanwhile, Isobel Hadley-Kamptz, a columnist for the respected centrist newspaper Dagens Nyheter, takes aim at Donald Trump in her article "Trump has always wanted Russia to win", accusing him of playing into Moscow's hands. She argues that pressuring Kyiv to make territorial concessions would threaten the security of Europe as a whole – a danger Sweden is well aware of.
During off-the-record meetings, we kept being asked the same questions: how to work as a journalist during a full-scale war, how to retain people in the profession and keep them alive, and how to deal with the challenges we face. The measures Sweden is taking now will undoubtedly help its society withstand the worst-case scenario.
Yet, looking at Sweden's peaceful, thriving streets, I had just one thought: I would not wish on anyone in the world what Ukraine is going through.
	
The trip to Stockholm took place as part of the Women Leaders in Media programme, organised by the NGO Women in Media with backing from International Media Support (IMS).
Khrystyna Golovko

articles.title: Finnish and Norwegian leaders discuss Ukraine peace with Putin as a source close to the Kremlin warns of escalating hybrid warfare with Europe
articles.body:
Finnish and Norwegian leaders discuss Ukraine peace with Putin as a source close to the Kremlin warns of escalating hybrid warfare with Europe
Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre spoke by phone with Vladimir Putin. Western leaders initiated the call to discuss Russia’s war against Ukraine and diplomatic efforts to end it.
The Finnish president’s office said the call was meant “to convey messages directly regarding future negotiations to help to end the war to President Putin” ahead of meetings to be held in Abu Dhabi. It was Putin’s first contact with European leaders supporting Ukraine since July 2025, when he spoke with French President Emmanuel Macron.
The Kremlin confirmed the call, saying Putin “assessed the current situation” in Ukraine and reminded participants of the “root causes of the conflict.” Putin also pointed to the “confrontational policy of EU and NATO countries, which is prolonging the fighting,” the Kremlin’s press service said.
Volodymyr Zelensky said Stubb and Støre briefed him on their call with Putin. “Alex and Jonas made it clear to the Russian leader that real de-escalatory steps are needed regarding our energy and infrastructure,” Zelensky said. He added that the Finnish and Norwegian leaders had discussed preparations for a trilateral meeting between negotiating teams from Ukraine, the United States, and Russia.
Stubb’s office said the call “was a follow-up of the meeting in Oslo on October 20 and held in consultation with Ukraine.” The Norwegian capital hosted talks that day between Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff and Zelensky, with Støre and Stubb also taking part. Witkoff then traveled to St. Petersburg to meet with Putin before returning to Oslo and flying home to the United States.
Those trips produced an agreement on a trilateral meeting between the United States, Ukraine, and Russia, to be held in Abu Dhabi. The meeting will take place after November 4, Putin aide Yuri Ushakov said. The day before, on November 3, the United States will hold midterm elections in which Republicans could lose their congressional majority.
Announcing the timing, Ushakov said the peace talks would also have to involve “all of Europe.” Europe has long sought a negotiator to represent the European Union’s interests in talks on ending the war between Russia and Ukraine.
Stubb has repeatedly been named as a candidate for the role, having built a good relationship with Trump, including on the golf course, and emerged as one of Trump’s main points of contact with European leaders. The Telegraph has also named Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, and Czech President Petr Pavel among the candidates.
After Stubb and Støre’s call with Putin, Frederiksen criticized the initiative, saying she was “skeptical” and that the talks had not been coordinated with other European leaders. She added that she sees no sign that Russia wants peace with Europe, either in the hybrid war that continues every day or in Ukraine.
The independent Russian political newsletter Faridaily says contacts between European leaders and the Kremlin amount to “a significant shift in position.” European leaders had “mostly preferred not to talk to Putin at all” since the war began.
However, a source close to the Kremlin said that “events are moving toward escalation, including an intensification of hybrid warfare with Europe.” According to the source, Putin is convinced NATO is waging a hybrid war against Russia and blames Ukraine’s European allies for “comprehensive assistance” in attacks on Russia, including helping identify targets and guide strikes.
A source close to the Kremlin told Reuters that Putin told Stubb and Støre that Russia would not abandon its goal of capturing all of the Donbas. The European leaders responded that a “just” peace was necessary, the source added.

Elon Musk argues that the threat of Russian anti-satellite attacks is a reason to restrict Starlink’s military use in Ukraine
Starlink service for Ukraine’s armed forces was restricted over fears that Russia would shoot down the company’s satellites, a post on X by SpaceX chief Elon Musk suggests. Musk was responding to a post about Russia’s ability to blow up satellites in space.
“This is indeed one of the main reasons that Starlink must remain a civilian operation,” Musk tweeted. “It can be used for infrastructure that is military, but it cannot be used for unequivocally offensive strikes that make it fair game to be struck back. An adversary blowing up Starlink satellites would create a domino effect of destruction that would generate a vast field of debris making space unusable.”
In mid-October, Ukraine’s armed forces encountered restrictions on their Starlink satellite terminals, specifically the military version, Starshield. Connections cut out when drones flew faster than 160 kilometers per hour (about 100 mph).
Western media reported that Musk himself had initiated the restrictions on Starlink service for the Ukrainian military. He later accused Ukraine of using Starlink for “offensive” drone strikes. Ukraine’s armed forces responded that this was “technically impossible,” since Starlink does not work over Russian territory.

articles.title: Norway says 'successful' cyberattacks against the country have tripled in last six months
articles.body:
The country's National Security Authority said the rapid growth of artificial intelligence technology also posed a "serious risk" to Norwegian businesses and organisations.
Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) said on Tuesday that the number of "successful" cyberattacks targeting Norwegian organisations had trebled in the last six months as it warned of a continued threat to national security.
In a new report, the NSM - which is involved in efforts to counter espionage and hybrid threats - said the country's defence industry and space sector were particularly exposed to cyber risk.
"This also applies to critical infrastructure and service providers to organisations that are important to national security," it said.
"NSM has not previously made this type of assessment public," director Arne Christian Haugstøyl added. "We are doing so now because it is absolutely necessary to strengthen both the resilience and the ability to handle cyber operations in Norwegian organisations."
The report follows increasing warnings across Europe of suspected Russian hybrid attacks, including cyber operations.
In August, Norwegian media reported that a Russian hacker group had declared war on Norway while also claiming responsibility for a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack that had reportedly impacted multiple government digital services.
In its report published on Tuesday, the NSM did not point to a specific actor but said that certain businesses and organisations were being increasingly subjected to reconnaissance and ransomware and DDoS attacks.
The agency also warned of the threat posed by artificial intelligence technology, which it said posed a "serious risk" to Norwegian businesses and organisations.
“AI analyzes large amounts of data and identifies vulnerabilities faster than humans have been able to," Haugstøyl said. "These vulnerabilities open up new opportunities for cyberattacks at a faster pace and on a larger scale.
"This means that the risk is increasing, and the pace at which security measures are implemented must be accelerated."

articles.title: Caught stealing: An employee of Russia’s top-secret Department K has been convicted of selling a classified database
articles.body:
On Sept. 10, the Khimki City Court in suburban Moscow sentenced Anton Nesterov, a senior operative of the Bureau of Special Technical Measures (BSTM) of Russia’s Ministry of Internal Affairs, to 13 years in a maximum-security penal colony. Nesterov was found guilty of selling a classified Federal Security Service (FSB) database to a hacker, taking a bribe, and gaining unlawful access to computer information. The defendant pleaded guilty only in part and refused to name his accomplices. However, The Insider has established Nesterov’s connections and learned additional details of his criminal case. The BSTM unit where Nesterov served is overseen by Department K of the FSB’s Economic Security Service and has a reputation as the most corrupt and scandal-ridden in the Russian law enforcement system.
The criminal case against Nesterov
According to the prosecution, Nesterov copied onto a flash drive a classified FSB database containing compromising material on the leadership of Russia’s Finance Ministry, the Central Bank, and several of the largest state banks, and then posted an advertisement for its sale on the internet. A hacker, whose name has not been disclosed, responded to the ad and offered 9 million rubles ($108,800) for the files.
From here, however, the accounts diverge. According to one version, FSB operatives supposedly detained the buyer before he could acquire the classified data. According to another, the hacker succeeded in buying the database, was subsequently detained, then struck a deal with investigators and testified against Nesterov.
Still though, according to The Insider’s source, the buyer was an informant from the hacker community cooperating with Department K of the FSB’s Economic Security Service (ESS), and in addition to the theft of the secret database, investigators looked into Nesterov’s involvement in extorting a large bribe from the management of the construction company PIK. After all, more than 20 different contacts labeled “PIK” were purportedly found in his phone.
The Insider previously reported on PIK owner Sergei Gordeev’s connections, and his real estate development company is at the heart of this story as well. In 2025, when the firm refused to pay a bribe, Nesterov allegedly organized a DDoS attack on the Lovit internet provider, which serves PIK’s new developments in Moscow and St. Petersburg. For unknown reasons though, this episode did not make it into the final version of the charges.
The criminal case was first heard at Moscow’s Basmanny Court. At the defense counsel’s request, the hearings were then moved to the Moscow Region city of Khimki, the defendant’s official place of residence (although Nesterov had lived for several years in the Edem gated community near Solnechnogorsk). Among those summoned for questioning was Nesterov’s older brother, Ilya, who works as an auditor at Sheremetyevo Airport. He told the investigator that he knew nothing about his brother’s double life.
The Khimki City Court, which sat behind closed doors, sentenced Nesterov to 13 years in a maximum-security penal colony. He will most likely serve his term in Penal Colony No. 11 in the city of Bor, Nizhny Novgorod Region, which holds former officers of the FSB, Main Intelligence Directorate (GRU), Federal Protective Service (FSO), Interior Ministry, and Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) — a penitentiary facility The Insider also previously reported on.
Nesterov’s career
Anton Nesterov was born in 1992 in Ulyanovsk and developed an interest in computers early on. As a young man, he worked as an engineer at the Signal plant. In 2014, he took his father’s advice and enrolled in the Voronezh Institute of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, joining the department of radio engineering and electronics — a program known for training students from Belarus, Tajikistan, Azerbaijan, Mongolia, and Angola, alongside Russians.
After the institute, Nesterov was assigned to the ministry’s Bureau of Special Technical Measures (BSTM), where he rose to become a senior operative at the 4th section of the 40th department, handling financial crimes committed with the use of information technology and working under the supervision of the FSB’s Department K.
The 40th department, where Nesterov served, is considered the most corrupt and scandal-ridden unit within the BSTM. “They control all the well-known hackers. The guys from the 40th department drive decrepit Soviet vehicles to work, while in their garages they have posh cars registered to relatives and mistresses,” a Ministry of Internal Affairs source told The Insider.
During interrogations, Nesterov refused to name accomplices and took all the blame. However, The Insider’s source is confident that the operative most likely had accomplices from the FSB or the BSTM: “He sat in the FSB compound on Bolshaya Lubyanka Street and worked in tandem with guys from the FSB. It is hard to believe that Anton pulled it all off alone.”
“He sat in the FSB compound on Bolshaya Lubyanka Street and worked in tandem with guys from the FSB. It is hard to believe that Anton pulled it all off alone”
Fugitives from the BSTM and mysterious deaths in Mexico
The Bureau of Special Technical Measures was established in 1992 to combat the illegal distribution of radio-electronic and special technical equipment, electronic payment fraud, terrorism, incitement of ethnic hatred, and child pornography online. It excels in various technological tricks for surveillance and data interception and has at its disposal several direction-finding vehicles with extendable antennas capable of eavesdropping on any cell phone from a distance of 20 km. As a rule, these minibuses and GAZelles are disguised as vehicles marked “Refrigerator repair” or “We install windows.” Some of these special vehicles have been transferred to the occupied territories of Ukraine to track phone calls.
How effective these devices are in practice, however, is unclear. Raisa Parshina, owner of the Far Eastern Transport Group, told The Insider that when her son Maxim was kidnapped in 2005 and a ransom of $7 million was demanded, acquaintances advised her to turn privately to the BSTM to triangulate the incoming numbers. She met with employees of the bureau and was told that a direction finder costs $10,000 a day. Parshina agreed, but a week later she was told that no results had been obtained.
Regional BSTM units operate in all the main directorates of Russia’s Ministry of Internal Affairs, also carrying out tasks for their colleagues at the FSB. Since the Bureau’s creation, nearly all key positions have been held by former FSB officers.
Since 2017, BSTM has been headed by Lieutenant General Mikhail Litvinov, who previously worked as deputy head of the FSB’s 12th Center — responsible for tapping phones, monitoring internet traffic, and intercepting information from technical communication channels. Litvinov’s office was located in downtown Moscow, at 26 Myasnitskaya Street, next door to three units of the FSB’s Operational Search Directorate (military units 52295, 96586, and 98933). For secrecy he was listed as head of the Center for Applied Research and supposedly engaged in studying public opinion.
Incidentally, since 2019 bailiffs from Moscow’s Zyuzino district have been unable to “squeeze” 46,668 rubles ($578) in taxes out of the general, left unpaid from his time working at the Center.
The appointment of Litvinov allowed the FSB to take the BSTM under its control, and the bureau expanded its remit to cover the wiretapping and surveillance of anti-Kremlin opposition figures and independent journalists.
However, in 2023 Litvinov was on the verge of dismissal after his subordinates — Georgy Satyukov, head of the 3rd section of the BSTM’s 40th department, and Dmitry Sokolov, a former colleague from Tyumen — fled abroad. According to the investigation, Sokolov’s brokering helped Satyukov secure a bribe of almost 5 billion rubles ($62 million) in bitcoin from Alexei Ivanov (Bilyuchenko), co-founder of the crypto exchange BTC, who was seeking the closure of a criminal case.
Satyukov received almost $62 million in bitcoin as a bribe for the closure of the criminal case against BTC founder Alexei Ivanov
The correspondence and phone conversations of Satyukov, Sokolov, and the crypto tycoon Ivanov were recorded by the FSB’s 12th Center, where General Litvinov used to serve. Shortly before their arrest, the corrupt operatives were tipped off by accomplices from the FSB and the BSTM, allowing them to flee the country.
It remained unclear how the fugitives crossed the border, since their passports were supposed to be kept in General Litvinov’s safe, and during questioning, the general denied having handed over the documents.
Following a suit by Russia’s Prosecutor General’s Office, the state seized millions of dollars’ worth of real estate from Satyukov: 13 apartments in Moscow and St. Petersburg (including a 200-square-meter unit in the elite Moscow complex Nezhinsky Kovcheg), and 11 non-residential properties in Saratov, Izhevsk, and the Sverdlovsk Region. His mansion in the UAE is currently frozen.
From Sokolov, the authorities confiscated: a nearly 500-square-meter apartment in St. Petersburg valued at 400 million rubles ($4.96 million), three luxury apartments on Kamenny Island, and a mansion in a historic district of the Petrograd Side. At the request of the Prosecutor General’s Office, the authorities in Dubai also froze Sokolov’s apartment in the Burj Khalifa tower.
Then, in 2024, Satyukov and Sokolov supposedly died in Mexico — one after the other, even if investigators suspect their deaths have been faked. In a conversation with The Insider, investigative journalist Andrei Zakharov said that phone billing records of the “dead” Satyukov and Sokolov feature the same BSTM operatives whom Nesterov called, along with three dozen alleged crypto figures, hackers, and businessmen from all over Russia.
Still, a source at the FSB told The Insider that after Nesterov’s imprisonment, BSTM head Litvinov is unlikely to keep his seat. Most likely, he will be given an order and sent off to a well-earned retirement.

articles.title: Guns fall silent around Russian-occupied Oleshky so its starving residents can get aid, but Russia’s guarantees remain secret
articles.body:
A ceasefire around Russian-occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast took effect at 03:00 on 27 October Kyiv time, and both sides were complying with the agreements, Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said. Russia’s Defense Ministry reported that its forces had stopped firing on the Kherson axis at 04:00 Moscow time, at the same moment.
Russia has kept Oleshky cut off for months. In June, the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine documented worsening shortages of food, medicine, and medical care there and in neighboring Hola Prystan. As of 8 October, Lubinets’ office still saw no practical breakthrough toward an organized evacuation, with 358 residents verified as needing help to leave. The ceasefire is the first step that has to hold before aid can go in and residents can leave, an operation Marc Beckman, the first lady’s chief adviser, expects to take five to seven days.
By 09:00 on 27 October, Russian forces were still observing the ceasefire, according to Pavlo Drohal, spokesperson for Ukraine’s 30th Marine Corps. Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Presidential Office, announced that the mission had begun and that Lubinets had gone to the site to coordinate it.
Ceasefire brought forward by two days
The White House announced on 23 October that First Lady Melania Trump had secured a localized ceasefire, set to begin on 29 October. The same evening, Russia’s chief of General Staff Valery Gerasimov announced a ceasefire on the Kherson axis from 27 October, with engineering reconnaissance and a secured route for a humanitarian convoy. Ukraine’s General Staff followed, introducing a ceasefire in a designated area from the same hour.
Beckman told Ukrinform on 26 October that Russia had moved the ceasefire two days earlier and extended it beyond Oleshky into Kherson Oblast. Lubinets said on 23 October that the mission should effectively begin on 29 October, after demining, adding that the date was not a matter of principle for either side.
A day after the announcement, Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova, who lead the two negotiating groups, confirmed the timing in an online meeting, he said. According to Lubinets, the agreement covers demining the road to Oleshky, delivering food, water, medicine, and hospital equipment, and safe movement for civilians.
Newsmax to document the operation
Meanwhile, Melania Trump said she had secured an “impartial American media organization” to accompany the Russian and Ukrainian teams. Beckman named it as Newsmax. He said he had worked directly with the channel’s owner, and that its journalists would record testimony as what he called neutral American observers.
Residents could leave for Ukraine or Russia, or stay, Beckman said. He added that Russia had assured Kyiv and Washington it would respect their choice of destination. Both governments asked him not to disclose what guarantees Russia gave or how violations would be handled, he said. He expects the operation to take five to seven days after 29 October, with an extension possible if both sides agree.
Diplomat doubts the truce will move peace talks
At the same time, Kostiantyn Yelisieiev, Ukraine’s ambassador to the EU in 2010–2015, told Radio NV the truce became possible only through the personal involvement of Donald and Melania Trump. The US president, he said, sees it as a way to show Americans he is bringing peace closer. He said he expects Russia to attempt provocations aimed at pushing residents toward the Russian side.
Yelisieiev said he does not share the optimism of those who think Oleshky could push the wider peace process forward. He compared it to the Black Sea grain corridor, a one-off arrangement that no longer works. He warned of a “diplomatic smokescreen”: Russia imitates negotiations while it keeps fighting, hoping Ukraine and its partners weaken over time.
A town under blockade
Oleshky lies on the left bank of the Dnipro, about 4 km from Kherson, and has been occupied since February 2022, Radio Svoboda reported. The White House says it had about 24,000 residents before the war and estimates 1,700 to 2,000 remain, mostly elderly, including about 50 children. Russian troops have also seized food dropped by Ukrainian drones, a local official said.
